subsubtopic: MR. ALLMAND-HAMILTON HARBOUR-NEWSPAPER REPORT ALLEGING RCMP INVESTIGATION DELAYED FOR POLITICAL REASONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege I wish to refer to two newspaper articles written by Claude Henault of the United Press, one appearing in the Montreal Gazette of Saturday, March 8, and the other appearing this morning, March 10. These articles might have appeared in other newspapers as well. In the first article of March 8 there is the following statement:
The investigation into the Hamilton Harbour Commission fraud scandal was delayed at least six months and perhaps one year while the RCMP waited for political permission to proceed.

subsubtopic: MR. ALLMAND-HAMILTON HARBOUR-NEWSPAPER REPORT ALLEGING RCMP INVESTIGATION DELAYED FOR POLITICAL REASONS
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: MR. ALLMAND-HAMILTON HARBOUR-NEWSPAPER REPORT ALLEGING RCMP INVESTIGATION DELAYED FOR POLITICAL REASONS
speechtext:
This is a completely false statement. I told the reporter on Friday that it was false. There was no negligent or deliberate delay in these investigations. It was officially launched on February 22, 1973, soon after I received a letter from the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) requesting such an investigation. It was proceeded with with all due dispatch, without any hindrance from any political source. This can be confirmed by the RCMP.
The RCMP communique issued on May 29, 1974, at which time charges were laid against five individuals, stating that the investigation was commenced in September, 1973, referred only to one aspect of the total investigation, for example, the particular investigation which lead to the five charges. But the investigation into the original allegations was started on February 22. This was explained to the reporter several times, but he negligently or deliberately ignored this fact.
I should, furthermore, point out to the House that a member of the Hamilton City Council approached the Hamilton detachment of the RCMP in September, 1972, with certain allegations of wrongdoing in the Hamilton Harbour Commission, but on examination the detachment felt that the matters involved were those matters which fell under the Criminal Code and, consequently, should be investigated by the Hamilton City Police or the Ontario Provincial Police.
We understand that the Hamilton Council member then approached the Hamilton City Police and the Ontario Provincial Police, but they did not have the resources to carry out the investigation and the Hamilton official came back to the RCMP at a later date. At this point the RCMP referred the matter to the Minister of Transport, who in turn wrote me requesting the investigation. I immediately turned the matter over to the RCMP and the investigation was started on February 22. There was no delay of six months to one year, as alleged in the article, while the RCMP waited for political approval. When political approval was asked, it was given immediately.
The second article appeared under the same reporter's name in the Gazette of this morning, March 10. The story reports that the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) has charged the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Liberal government with covering up the politically explosive Hamilton harbour dredging contracts scandal. I do not know if the reporter reports the hon. member as the same reporter likes to report me; but in any case, if the hon. member did make that charge, I should like to ask him to repeat it in the House of Commons and defend it in the usual way.

subsubtopic: MR. ALLMAND-HAMILTON HARBOUR-NEWSPAPER REPORT ALLEGING RCMP INVESTIGATION DELAYED FOR POLITICAL REASONS
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: MR. ALLMAND-HAMILTON HARBOUR-NEWSPAPER REPORT ALLEGING RCMP INVESTIGATION DELAYED FOR POLITICAL REASONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MR. ALLMAND-HAMILTON HARBOUR-NEWSPAPER REPORT ALLEGING RCMP INVESTIGATION DELAYED FOR POLITICAL REASONS
speechtext:
If the Solicitor General is able to satisfy the House and the country on two points, then I am sure this whole matter could be clarified. The first point is: why the delay from the time of the inquiry in Hamilton to the commencement of the inquiry into the lie d'Orleans contract? The second question is: why would the RCMP, if they wanted to commence an inquiry into dredging contracts in the province of Quebec, go to the Minister of Transport?
The Minister of Transport has no jurisdiction whatsoever over the RCMP. The only minister to whom the RCMP could report regarding any apparent irregularity in contracts anywhere in Canada involving the federal government would be the minister responsible, and that is the Solicitor General. But the RCMP did not do that, and we have the minister's own words for it in the House on March 4 in reply to my question. I asked the minister:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask a final supplementary question. Did the RCMP extend the investigation into the lie d'Orleans contract on their own initiative, or were they requested so to do by the Minister of Transport?
The minister's rather intriguing reply was:
Mr. Speaker, they were requested by the Minister of Transport to begin investigations in Hamilton. Once the RCMP found there was evidence which led them to Quebec City, they reported to the Minister of Transport, and he told them to go full speed ahead in Quebec City as well.
Why would the RCMP have to report to the Minister of Transport? Why would they need his permission to go full speed ahead in investigations into very serious, alleged criminal charges? I submit that this whole affair has evidence, albeit circumstantial, of an attempt at least to confine this investigation to Hamilton, and when that failed the attempt was made to try to cover it up. Until the minister is ready to answer our questions, I am afraid he is leaving himself and his colleagues in the government open to suspicion.

speakeroldname: Hon. John N. Turner (Minister of Finance):
speechtext: A significant portion of time spent reviewing provisions of the Income Tax Act is devoted to problems of retirement income, including, of course, pension plans. However, it should be noted that the four areas mentioned are covered to a major degree by provincial legislation and by federal legislation in acts other than the Income Tax Act. subtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP-SUGGESTION GOVERNMENT MAKE SERIOUS OFFER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have said many times that the House of Commons is not the place to negotiate. I can repeat what I have already said. Our final offer was much lower than the majority conciliation board report. Eventually, in order to arrive at a settlement, we concluded it would be good for the government to accept the report of the president of the conciliation board. If the union had acted in the same manner in that conflict, there would have been no strike at all.

subtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP-SUGGESTION GOVERNMENT MAKE SERIOUS OFFER

subtopic: STRIKE OF GENERAL LABOUR AND TRADES GROUP-SUGGESTION GOVERNMENT MAKE SERIOUS OFFER
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it was exactly for that reason we went back to the negotiating table last Friday. We made new offers over the weekend. INVESTIGATION INTO DREDGING CONTRACTS-REASON FOR FAILURE TO ACT ON REQUEST BY CITY OF HAMILTON IN 1972 FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question for the Solicitor General. Keeping in mind that the minister indicated the city of Hamilton had the local police as well as the OPP involved with the investigators in connection with the Hamilton harbour, which indicates that something was going on, and keeping in mind that the city of Hamilton asked this government by way of a resolution on October 31, 1972, to conduct a full-scale open inquiry, can the minister now advise why that request by the city of Hamilton was refused at that time, particularly when we note that an investigation had been asked for subsequently, sometime around January 8, January 12, January 26, leading up to February 22, 1973. Why was the request by the city of Hamilton not recognized at that time, because it seems they knew what was going on and were seeking assistance.

subtopic: INVESTIGATION INTO DREDGING CONTRACTS-REASON FOR FAILURE TO ACT ON REQUEST BY CITY OF HAMILTON IN 1972 FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is true that in September, 1972 some person or persons from the Hamilton city council came to the RCMP detachment in Hamilton with certain allegations of wrongdoing with respect to the Hamilton harbour. On examination of those allegations by the local detachment, the local detachment felt these were matters which gave rise to accusations under the Criminal Code and in the ordinary course such investigations should be undertaken either by the Hamilton City Police or by the Ontario Provincial Police. For that reason, the officials went to the OPP and the Hamilton City Police but the latter felt they did not have the resources necessary to carry on that kind of investigation-this is what I am told. So, the Hamilton officials went back to the RCMP, and the RCMP said that since this was a case which was usually dealt with by another police force they would refer the matter to higher officials. This they did, and on balance the RCMP decided that they would investigate after consulting with the Ministry of Transport, even though it was a case which would normally be dealt with under the authority of a provincial government. They did decide to investigate in any case, because the others were not ready to do so.

subtopic: INVESTIGATION INTO DREDGING CONTRACTS-REASON FOR FAILURE TO ACT ON REQUEST BY CITY OF HAMILTON IN 1972 FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext: It seems to me there was a lot of action in the City of Hamilton in and around September, 1972. I want to know why it took the government so long to involve the RCMP. We find out, now, that they were not engaged in a full investigation until February of 1973.

subtopic: INVESTIGATION INTO DREDGING CONTRACTS-REASON FOR FAILURE TO ACT ON REQUEST BY CITY OF HAMILTON IN 1972 FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
The government did not interfere. It was not even aware of what was going on in the Hamilton detachment at that time. It was the Hamilton detachment of the RCMP itself which came to the decision that the matter was not within its jurisdiction at that stage. That was the judgment based on the facts as presented to the detachment. The matter only reached the level of officials in Ottawa, and the RCMP in Ottawa, at a later date. At that time, as the hon. member knows, an election was in progress, or had just been completed, ministers had been changed, and so on. But as soon as possible, after the matter had been brought to the attention of Ottawa, a

letter was sent to me by the Minister of Transport and the investigation was under way.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this case has just been brought to my attention and I have requested the full preparation of the file so I can review it. He has no authority extended to him by the House to hide such information with the words:

I raised a similar matter to this a week or so ago. I think we have the right to know who did it, who recommended the projects, and all the details. speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext: With the greatest of regrets I must differ with the last statement of the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Cossitt). As the hon. member well knows, the action on his part may be the subject of debate, which it surely is, but under the rules as they are presently drawn, it does not constitute a question of privilege.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PRESENT CO-ORDINATED TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
That this House condemns the government's failure to present a co-ordinated transportation policy.
March 10, 1975

He said: Mr. Speaker, I believe the timing of this motion bears some significance for it was one year almost to this day-on March 7, 1974-that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) in a speech to this House said the following, as recorded at page 267 of Hansard:
We do not have what we can call a real policy for the future. If I stay in this post I shall surely ask the authority of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the cabinet to try to elaborate this kind of policy so that we know where we are going.
Perhaps I should repeat the last phrase, "so that we know where we are going," because in a nutshell it summarizes the state of affairs in which we find ourselves. Judged on its performance, this government and this minister simply do not know where they are going in developing a national transportation policy.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PRESENT CO-ORDINATED TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PRESENT CO-ORDINATED TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
The minister went on to say, as recorded at page 268 of Hansard:
Something we do not have is a real policy and I hope that sooner, rather than later, it will be possible to have such a policy.
The question that one must ask is this: after we have gone through a general election campaign in which the subject of transportation was one of the major issues, after the Liberal Party received a mandate, after the Speech from the Throne, and after a signal of willingness from all parties of the House to co-operate in developing a worthy national objective, where is the government's policy on transportation? We still have nothing that resembles, in the slightest sense, a comprehensive, national transportation policy. In fact, by the minister's own admission on January 23, 1975, as recorded at page 2530 of Hansard, there was then still no over-all policy and the means of transportation had not been integrated.
That is the purpose of the motion I have introduced in the name of my party today. This is our way of registering our protest against this government and against this minister for their inaction and for their disjointed approach to this very important and vital matter. Where are we going, and what has happened? The minister indicated himself on March 7, 1974, that transportation was in a mess. On October 3, 1974, in another speech to the House, he reiterated that statement by saying, in reference to his speech of March 7:
There is not a single sentence in it that needs to be changed.
That was said in October. It is significant that at the time the minister first made his comments about no policy and the fact that transportation was in a mess, he was praised by the news media for his candour, his frankness and his originality. However, as time passed the phrase was reused and it began to wear thin. We found the minister referring to that phrase only on rare occasions when he was in a state of depression or flippancy, as he did on January 22, 1975, as recorded at page 2509 of Hansard-almost a year later. In response to a question posed by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Hogan), he repeated that we have no over-all policy and, further, he agreed that transportation was still a mess, "and more than you think".
Transportation
This simply means, in the words of the minister, that no progress has been made. The minister can shake his head in the negative: I do not know what interpretation he puts on those phrases. But what is more astonishing is the fact that the minister attempts to blame the Conservatives for the mess, as he did on January 22, 1975, when he said as reported at page 2509 of Hansard:
-while the Conservative Party was in power they did nothing to correct this mess.
That was twelve years ago. I should not have to remind the minister of some of the bold initiatives which were taken during that administration. I think the minister knows very well, and surely he should not have to be reminded, that it was a Liberal government of which he was a member which developed the present National Transportation Act which to this day provides the umbrella of transportation policy in Canada and from which he now, for the sake of expedience, conveniently attempts to dissociate himself.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PRESENT CO-ORDINATED TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: We all know that the minister is charming and delightful; he is disarming and candid. But I say to him in all sincerity that whether he is French, English, German or Polish, he has not proved himself to be competent in his portfolio, and until he proves otherwise my view will remain the same. The Ministry of Transport and the minister himself can best be summarized as being in a state of suspended confusion with regard to Canada's transportation system. One can only sympathize with the very hard working, dedicated people attached to that department who have been starved of leadership and direction and who have been promised government leadership but, instead, have received nothing. I am not alone in reaching that conclusion. A well known and well respected journalist, Mr. W. A. Wilson-I presume the minister would not place him in the same category as Mr. Fisher or Mr. Barkway-in the February 3 issue of the Montreal Star headlines it as "A transport policy run-around, nothing achieved".

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PRESENT CO-ORDINATED TRANSPORTATION POLICY

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PRESENT CO-ORDINATED TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
That may or may not be a point of privilege, but I simply want to reiterate the fact that there are some journalists who are objective. The Minister of Transport may have his views and opinions on some of them, but I believe the person whom I have just quoted, namely, Mr. Wilson, is indeed an objective, well respected and well known journalist and I think his comments and summary should not go unnoticed.

Let us look for a moment at some of the commitments and promises advanced during the election campaign of 1974. It seems to me that the minister has a short memory, as do some of his colleagues who support him. Their objective seems to be to say anything that will win votes, and hope that the opposition and the people will forget. But we shall not forget the promises that were made; we shall not forget the commitments. We shall remind this minister and this government, at every opportunity, of the commitments and promises they made to the Canadian people.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PRESENT CO-ORDINATED TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PRESENT CO-ORDINATED TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
I wish to put a few things on the record which are included in the $2 billion transportation package unveiled back on June 19, 1974. I will quote in some detail because it seems the minister must be reminded of some of the commitments and promises which were made. The June 19 press release of the minister, given at a news conference, reads as follows:
Transport minister Jean Marchand today announced sweeping changes in the institutional structures which manage Canadian transportation, a radical departure from past transportation philosophy and a comprehensive set of new transportation programs for Canada. "These changes and these programs are going to move Canada toward world leadership in the use and construction of passenger and freight transportation systems. We are reaching for world leadership in quality equipment and systems", Mr. Marchand said.
Canada is going to be given a new generation of management mechanisms-and a new set of programs-for transportation ...
The government is going to develop a new relationship with the Canadian Transport Commission, and with the private sector and Crown corporations which provide transportation to Canada, to ensure that the government can review and co-ordinate plans formulated by our transportation industry. The Minister of Transport will have all the authority he requires to put policy into place and make it work, and to ensure key national priorities are not sacrificed to other considerations. It will be the federal government, on behalf of the Canadian people, that will play the leading role in managing transportation policy in Canada.
It goes on to say that a Canadian passenger transportation corporation will be brought into existence, and later it
says:
Federal support will be made available to municipalities for both the design and financing of top quality Canadian designed and built city and suburban transit systems.
Air services to Canada's populated remote areas will be improved. "In effect, we are moving toward abolishing the term 'isolated' from the Canadian vocabulary as far as Canada's populated remote communities are concerned," Mr. Marchand said. "We are going to guarantee first class citizenship to residents of Canada's remote areas through equal quality transportation networks."
A second major priority of these new transportation policies will be the redevelopment and upgrading of Canada's rail and port systems so that Canada can handle the doubling of its exports expected within the next seven to ten years. A central part of this thrust will be a "reserve freight car fleet" ... a new "national freight car leasing corporation."
This is hilarious. It continues:
In the west, railway access from the prairies to the west coast and to Thunder Bay is going to be strongly upgraded. This program will involve strengthened rail roadbeds, some double tracking and eventual electrification. The government will be launching a comprehensive program to improve railway access to the ports of Vancouver and Prince Rupert...
March 10, 1975

The third major priority of these new transportation policies is the removal of regional inequities in freight rates. Mr. Marchand said it has been demonstrated over the past six years that the principle of competition on which Canadian freight rates has been based, that is, competition between different modes of transport supposedly resulting in fair and low rates, has not worked for many areas in Canada. The Liberal government will adopt the principle of consistent and equitable pricing of freight rates rather than the old "what the traffic will bear" principle. "This will be a dramatic change ... a "Transportation Information Act" will be introduced ...
New legislation will make it clear that henceforth the Canadian Transport Commission will be exercising its powers within the guidelines of government policy. The CTC will function less as a "court of record" and apply regulations in a fashion that encourages the positive development of the Canadian transportation system ... "Canadians deserve a transportation system that matches the imagination of the country-and they are going to get one," Mr. Marchand emphasized.
It goes on to deal with urban transportation policies and then continues:
The Liberal government will ensure adequate funding for capital expenditures from both public and private sources to meet the public's minimum capacity and service expectations in transportation.
I could go on and on. But what happened to those lofty proposals? They were lost somewhere between the election and the Speech from the Throne. The Speech from the Throne advanced about ten specific commitments, but to this date action has been taken on only one, Bill C-48, the amendments to the Railway Act. The opposition co-operated in the passage of that bill by allowing limited time for debate in the House. It was considered in committee at two short meetings and has been proceeded with. If this were such a priority item, one might ask why it took so long for it to be introduced.
The Speech from the Throne referred to grain handling and the urgency of facilitating grain movement. But no plan of action has been brought forward. We must give the government credit for moving to end the strike which stopped grain shipments last September, but we must also ask why it hesitates to act now. Grain has been tied up on the west coast since February 17. Is it not considered essential to move it because there are two different parties involved, or is it because the government has a policy of selectivity in disputes of this nature?
The situation is urgent and people in the world are starving. In the port of Vancouver, the Liberian tanker which was destined to carry the largest grain cargo ever sent to the hungry and starving people of Bangladesh remains tied up, half loaded. Close to 50 ships are waiting now, and demurrage charges are piling up all the time. In the last year, demurrage charges to farmers in Canada were $17 million. Grain has not moved for three weeks, Mr. Speaker, and sales are being lost. The forward sales arranged last year were made on the basis of price set at the date of delivery. We all know that wheat prices have dropped significantly over the past 60 days. It has been estimated that Canadian producers will lose in the order of $200 million or $300 million because of the delay in delivery.
Canada's economy is being severely impaired. In total, the public interest is being severely undermined. I believe it is time for the government to act. In my view-and this is only my view-it is time the movement of grain in this country were classified as an essential service and the right to strike withdrawn.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PRESENT CO-ORDINATED TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PRESENT CO-ORDINATED TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
I say this after a great deal of deliberation, Mr. Speaker, because of the importance of the grain economy to this country and the importance of our international reputation. I do not believe we can tolerate this situation any longer. Surely when lives and Canada's reputation are affected it is time to put an end to this stupidity and nonsense. We must be the laughing-stock of all nations. Surely we can manage our affairs with much more command, with more order and sensibility. The government must seriously consider ways to stop this horrendous waste now and in the future. For goodness sake, in the name of humanity let us inject some sensibility into the handling of this important matter. This must come, and it can only come through government leadership.
Some things have been done by this Minister of Transport, and I want to give credit where credit is due. There have been a number of studies-the roadbed study, Alberta's equitable pricing technique, Manitoba's destination rate principle-but of all these studies and seminars only one has been tabled, and that was done before the committee. Why all this secrecy? These studies were paid for with public funds and were supposed to be for the benefit of all Canadians. It seems to me that members of this House are entitled to this information, Mr. Speaker. But this is another example of the government's contempt for members of this House. Surely, if we are to consider national transportation and the objectives of a realistic and comprehensive policy, all members should have the benefit of studies that have been carried out to date.
There have been meetings in the west and in the mari-times, technical committees and federal-provincial committees. The minister in charge of the Wheat Board even has his own study group apparently working in isolation from the others. But we have not seen any progress reports, Mr. Speaker. What are they doing? What guidelines do they operate under? We get the odd communique, but basically this information is for political consumption. A communique issued on February 24 was described by some as a breakthrough, but in reality it was only a regrouping of anomalies and amounted to nothing more than a repeat of a commitment given two years ago.
The best we can say is that the steps taken to date represent a hodge-podge, a patchwork of proposals without any national direction or purpose. The same disjointedness and inconsistency applies when members seek information in the House or in committee. Anyone who wants to review the situation should read the debate that took place on the estimates on October 23, or the minutes of some of the committee hearings. It is no wonder members of the House are frustrated. When we get into major items such as the Crowsnest freight rates, rail line abandonment or policy issues we only get evasive or flippant answers; and, when we speak to different ministers we get different answers.
So far as the Crowsnest freight rates are concerned, the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board is calling for a complete review. The Minister of Transport has indicated that no officials in his department are reviewing the Crowsnest freight rates, and that certainly there is no

March 10, 1975
Transportation
intention to modify them. So we have that double standard. Then there is the rail line abandonment issue which must be considered. About 6,000 miles of trackage is due for study and review. We get one answer from the Minister of Transport and another from the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. The question of the rape-seed freight rate case has been the subject of consideration by the CTC since 1970. An interim decision was handed down in 1973. There was an appeal to the cabinet in March of 1974, but still no action has been taken.
The minister asks where is our policy. When we look at the question of air policy, where is their policy, Mr. Speaker? So far as third level air carrier service is concerned, on March 7, 1974, the minister stated, as recorded at page 267 of Hansard, that we would be silly to establish a third carrier air system. Then during the election campaign we were told that there would be a third level air carrier service developed in Canada, engineered, managed and with assistance provided by Air Canada. Last Friday the Minister of Transport as reported at page 3893 of Hansard, said:
We are now formulating a comprehensive system, a third level of regional carriers.
There is inconsistency on the part of the Canadian Transport Commission, the minister and the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). The CTC is evidently operating in a vacuum with respect to regional and third level carriers. There is no pattern to any of the actions that either the commission or the ministry have taken to date. We have unfulfilled commitments, no planning, no co-ordination- just ad hoc, political gimmickry.
It is, surely, essential that this country be linked by and served with the safest, most efficient and effective transportation system known. It is as important as, if not more important than, issues such as energy, communications, health and welfare, the economy, the constitution or the Mackenzie Valley pipeline. I mention these specific items because they have been the subject of consideration by first ministers' conferences, federal-provincial conferences and national forums. Transportation is by no means a small item. We spend well in excess of $15 billion a year on transportation, more than on food and the federal health budget. Surely we must stop dealing with transportation in little bits and pieces here and there.
Having regard to the importance of transportation to this country, the link it provides in maintaining national unity and the role it plays in achieving social and economic justice, I believe the time has come to convene a national conference on transportation to deal with this national problem in a national way. It should be a conference that will draw together the various provincial and federal governments, the various modes of transportation, all the elements of our transportation system and those who are specialists in the field. I think such a conference should be broad enough to allow input from all interested parties. The federal government would naturally have to define the national goals and objectives-the guidelines, if you wish-and serve as a leadership catalyst.
In this over-all review, with all elements working together, it seems to me that a broad, national consensus may be achieved that would serve as a national instrument for achieving unity and national purpose. I admit it

might be difficult to achieve such consensus, but I do believe it is possible even though it is a very complex subject. I believe it can be achieved, I believe it should be achieved, and I recommend this suggestion to the minister.
I should like to continue, Mr. Speaker, but I see that my time has practically elapsed. I will close simply by saying that the subject of transportation is indeed a very serious one. It is something that should not become a game of political gimmickry; it is an issue that is far too serious for such tactics. In my opinion, transportation in this country is at a critical juncture. It requires strong, determined leadership-not phony showmanship or political gamesmanship.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PRESENT CO-ORDINATED TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want first of all to say that I agree with the motion before the House today. I believe the issue of transportation is very complex and complicated, and is very badly coordinated and planned throughout the economy. Transportation is central to the future development of this country. It is essential to the present economy and to almost every walk of life. In fact, if you examine the transportation system in this country you find that the minister was not only right when he said that, essentially, transportation is in a mess, but historically it has served the interests of the CPR and the huge corporations in terms of facilitating their profit motives rather than providing the people of Canada with service, it has perpetrated a hinterland economy to the detriment of areas like the north, the prairies, many parts of Quebec and the Atlantic provinces and to the favour of the golden horseshoe area and the lower mainland of British Columbia, to give two examples.
I should like to give some examples later in my remarks of how our transportation and freight rates systems discriminate against western Canada and the prairies, but I think transportation itself typifies or personifies the very nature of our unplanned economy. We find ourselves often subject to the many whims of international economics, particularly those of the United States. We are suffering, in this country, from unemployment and inflation but many of our problems stem from the fact that we have a transportation system that is inefficient and does not allow certain areas of the country to thrive as they should. These are anomalies that must be removed.
I think the greatest tool to fashion a regional development policy in this country is massive subsidization of freight rates in the maritimes, many parts of Quebec, the north and the prairies. The present freight rates structure discriminates against the processing of raw materials in those areas and favours such processing in the golden horseshoe, particularly the city of Toronto. It is cheaper to ship livestock from Saskatchewan to Toronto than it is to ship the processed product. Therefore, this means we are exporting jobs from Saskatchewan to Toronto.
We in this House must get the government to become serious about transportation and to pour hundreds of millions of dollars into equalizing freight rates and removing these anomalies. Perhaps we should favour areas that are now discriminated against. We must have equality of conditions if the maritimes are to be developed. One of the first steps we must take is to provide potential industries in these areas with equalized freight rates to enable them to ship finished goods from the maritimes, the north or the
March 10, 1975

prairies at basically the same cost as shipping products from one of the larger urban centres.
We should have, as minimum objective in this country, a freight rates structure that is no more expensive for any part of the country than the average rates in the United States. As long as we do not have this, there is no way we will be able to compete with industries in the United States. For years Canada has been an exporter of raw materials and an importer of finished goods. We have been exporting more capital than has come in by way of new investment. We have been exporting jobs because we do not refine and manufacture our raw materials. Before we can attempt to do this in a planned industrial economy, we need a freight rates system that does not discriminate against manufacturing goods. Indeed, we should provide incentives not to discriminate.
For the last two years the government has been saying that transportation is in a mess. When the minister first said that a year or two ago, I was very pleased by his honesty, frankness and candour before the House. But I have now reached the point where I am becoming very frustrated at the lack of action. The minister has had about two years to go through his department, study it, meet with ministers and governments across the country and find out what is wrong with transportation. But nothing has happened. There has been no concrete activity on the part of the government during the last two years.
I want to read into the record some statements made by the government many months ago, statements they are still making in the House today. I go back to the throne speech after the 1972 election when a minority government was elected. In the January 4 speech, the government proposed a western economic opportunities conference. One of the goals was-
-an improvement in the total transportation system so basic to overcoming the problems of distance.
On March 20, 1973, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mar-chand) said in this House:
I am as amazed as anyone in the House when I come across freight rates that are higher for goods transported to Regina than for those transported to Vancouver or elsewhere. I can understand it in the context of the capitalist system... Anyone who believes in profits and in the private enterprise system knows that any company tries for the highest yield that the market can absorb. And that is the only valid explanation ... it is a provocation ... the present situation is frequently intolerable.
I agree with the minister. The present system is based on so-called competition, the free enterprise philosophy. We in the prairies have no competition. We cannot ship our cattle by air to the markets in the east. We cannot ship our goods by river, lake or ocean. There is no competition with the railways. That is why it costs more for people on the prairies to have many goods shipped to them from Toronto than it costs people in Vancouver to have goods shipped from that city. We have a market that is growing. Our only alternative is to have a government with the guts to carry on and do the things the Minister of Transport talked about in this House a year or so ago. He does not have the guts to do them. All he does is talk. In the March 21, 1974, issue of the Globe and Mail, the minister is quoted as saying:
Transportation
We don't know where we are going.
It is obvious the minister does not know. On June 12, during the last election campaign, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) spoke in Edmonton about our outmoded transportation system, that some planning is needed, we cannot rely only on competition, and so on. We still have no concrete action from this government. In the Speech from the Throne at the opening of the thirtieth parliament there was a repetition of what had been said a year and a half earlier. On January 22, 1975, the minister said in this House:
We have no over-all policy ... It still is a mess, and more than you think.
As I said at the outset, I was willing to tolerate the minister saying that when he first took over the department. However, he has been Minister of Tranport for over two years, and if it was a mess when he took over two years ago, why has he not done something about it? I know it is a very complex, massive department, but why have we not had the changes the minister talked about when he took over the department? Freight rates are still rising, anomalies are still increasing, discrimination is escalating. I want to put on record some of the anomalies and discriminatory freight rates to which we in the prairies are subjected. The Minister of Tranport and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) will be participating in this debate. They must understand how the sort of freight rates which we have discriminate against various regions.
With regard to canned foodstuffs, to ship 100,000 pounds from southern Ontario to Vancouver costs $2.57 per hundredweight. To ship the same amount of foodstuffs to Saskatoon, which is on the main CNR line, costs $2.75 per hundredweight. It costs almost 20 cents more per hundredweight to ship about half the distance. Why does that anomaly exist? The Minister of Transport and the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion both know this. How can we eliminate regional inequality if the freight rate structure, which is the backbone of this country, has these built-in discriminations?
To ship an 80,000 pound lot of packaged foodstuffs from southern Ontario to Vancouver costs $2.43 per hundredweight. To ship the same amount of the same kind of goods to Saskatoon costs $2.93 per hundredweight, 50 cents more. Because of the way freight rates are set up, it might be cheaper to ship from southern Ontario to Vancouver and then reship back to Saskatoon. After two years in office, how can this minister still go on saying, in effect, "The damn thing is still a mess and we cannot do anything about it"? Where is the minister's intestinal fortitude? Why can't he stand up to the CNR, the CPR and others in the transportation field and make them do something about the blatant anomalies that exist in the freight rates system?
I now go to the open tariffs which took effect on March 1, 1975, just a few days ago. They widen, instead of close, the gap in discrimination against Saskatchewan. I wish to deal with the cost of shipping live cattle versus dressed or slaughtered beef. The rates from Saskatoon to either Toronto or Montreal are the same. The old rate for live cattle was $3.24 per hundredweight. As of March 1 it was increased to $4.23 per hundredweight. If the cattle are

March 10, 1975
Transportation
slaughtered and processed in Saskatchewan, providing jobs for people there, the rate as of March 1 is $5.40 per hundredweight, compared with the old rate of $4.15 per hundredweight. Why does the Minister of Transport tolerate that type of discrepancy?
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion professes to be getting rid of regional discrimination in this country. However, it now costs $1.17 per hundredweight more to ship dressed beef to Toronto. Any company engaged in the business of packing beef will obviously locate in Toronto or Montreal. That is not being anti-Canadian; it is sound economics. Obviously, any such operation would be expanded in central Canada because the freight rate structure is designed for them, not the people in the prairies, those in much of Quebec, in the north or the Atlantic provinces. These anomalies must be cleared up very quickly.
I will give two or three more examples. Iron and steel articles such as bars, rods, plates and studs can be shipped in 80,000-pounds lots from Hamilton to Vancouver for $2.43 per hundredweight under the new freight rate structure. The rate to Saskatoon is $2.84. To ship the same goods on the same line costs 40 cents per hundredweight more to ship to Saskatoon than it does to Vancouver. Why is that not changed? It is for this reason I have no confidence in the government's transportation policies or the handling of its affairs by the Minister of Transport.
Let us now look at more agreed charges. To ship a 75,000-pound lot of chemicals such as calcium carbide from Niagara Falls or Shawinigan to Vancouver costs $2.63 per hundredweight. The rate to Saskatoon is $3.12 per hundredweight. There is a difference of 30 or 40 per cent. I am not against the city of Vancouver. What I am saying is that freight rates should be lower for shorter hauls. Saskatoon and Regina are about two-thirds of the way to Vancouver, yet the freight rate for the same product on the same rail line is higher. That does not make sense: it is blatant discrimination against the prairies.
I could give other examples such as phosphates and sulphates which can be shipped to Vancouver at a lower rate than to Saskatchewan and, indeed, to many parts of Manitoba. The minister understands the situation. He knows the present freight rates structure is controlled by the railway companies, the private corporation. He knows they do not serve the majority of the regions of this country. Why does he not change it? Why does he not tell the CN and CP that there should no longer be anomalies in the freight rates structure? It should be equalized across Canada. If that were done, this country could be developed from coast to coast.
Why do we have to crowd our people into two or three large centres instead of dispersing our population around the country? And you will not be able to do that, no matter how much money DREE pumps into Newfoundland or other areas, if you continue to have a freight rates structure that discriminates against the very areas that DREE puts money into. It just won't work, Mr. Speaker. Why doesn't the minister-and I think that philosophically he believes it-nationalize the CPR and have one efficient transportation system in this country? We do not have

competing sewers. We do not have competing roads. Why don't we have one railway system?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PRESENT CO-ORDINATED TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: Why don't we have one political party?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PRESENT CO-ORDINATED TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
I do not think railways are there to make a profit. It should be a service to the people of this country. Why have two competing airlines. Why not have one Air Canada that has all the routes in this country? I think the minister made a comment about this when he spoke the other day. CPR often has the very lucrative routes in this country. Air Canada is serving many areas of the country where you wouldn't have service if it were not for the publicly-owned airline. So I very strongly urge this minister to follow his own gut instincts and nationalize the CPR into one comprehensive transportation system that is efficient, that is run with a tough, efficient manager for and on behalf of all the people of this country.
Pour into that transportation system hundreds of millions of dollars. Subsidize freight rates in areas where they need support. Provide equality of conditions in the mari-times, the north, the prairies and other regions which I have mentioned. Unless you do that, Mr. Speaker, you are not going to develop this country. Unless you do that you will continue to have unemployed, because it is just not worth processing our own goods in our own country. Unless you do that you are not going to have the political sovereignty to make a lot of the economic decisions we must make if we are to plan our country. Unless you do that you can no longer have a national development plan to put more people into areas where they are needed, and slow down growth in areas where growth is occurring too quickly.
I am sure people in Toronto would like to see growth in that city slowed down and rationalized. They would like to see some of their growth and industry go to the north, to the prairies or to the eastern part of this country. But that will not happen as long as we have a government which believes in the centralization of all industry in this country into central Canada, the golden horseshoe, as governments have done ever since confederation.
So, Mr. Speaker, I hope the minister, when he replies tonight, will agree to some basic changes in the transportation system, some of the things that I have talked about and some of the things to which the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) has referred. I hope he will also look at the grain handling system: we are having many problems there. Also, we have rail line abandonment; about one-third of the rail lines may be abandoned after January 1, 1976. we have a grain handling system that is inefficient mainly because the railways aren't repairing the tracks and maintaining them. They feel they don't make enough money out of handling grain.
We have many many problems in the west, problems that we must solve if we are to preserve the rural community from which some of us come. We must also make it very clear that the Crowsnest pass agreement which was made back in the 1800s must be upheld. The Crowsnest pass agreement is God in the west, and once again I tell the Minister of Transport that if he tampers with it, then he is tampering with something that everyone in western Canada will fight him for all the way down the line. So I
March 10, 1975

hope he reaffirms his intention not to tamper with the Crowsnest pass agreement when he speaks in the House later this evening.
Mr. Speaker, there are many things I could say. However, I realize that my time is up and I want, in closing, to ask the minister to respond very sincerely to many of the points we have raised. When he replies tonight, I ask him not to raise some of the old bogeymen, not to treat it as a personal attack upon his character, but to take it as constructive criticism of his department and the policies of the Government of Canada which most of us in the opposition see as falling short of what they should be. I know that many Liberals in all parts of Canada agree with me in that respect.
If we are to plan this country for the twenty-first century, for those who come after us, we must start with a transportation system that is publicly-owned, efficient, serving all the people, and subsidized in order to serve the whole country equally from coast to coast.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald C. Jamieson (Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PRESENT CO-ORDINATED TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am sure nothing could more graphically demonstrate the complexities of trying to devise in this country a cohesive transportation policy than the differences in approach taken by the first two speakers. The Conservative Party has put down the motion. The New Democratic Party, announcing that it will support it, then proceeds to demonstrate in the most graphic fashion imaginable that the elements the NDP would put into a national transportation policy would be totally rejected by the Conservative Party.
For example, just a moment ago when the spokesman for the NDP called for the nationalization of Canadian Pacific, I heard murmurs of indignation among Conservative Party members. Yet nationalization is the basic plan of the NDP program.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PRESENT CO-ORDINATED TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext: The motion is an attack on your policy; that is the point.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PRESENT CO-ORDINATED TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
I am sure that when the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) replies, as he will later in this debate, he will be perfectly able to defend himself. I say this with particular regard to some of the suggestions which have been made as to his intestinal fortitude and the like. I do not intend to deal with the broad spectrum of issues which have been raised; I shall confine my remarks to the aspects which concern regional development.
A number of speakers, including the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), have acknowledged the element of regional development which exists in any transportation policy. It is one which we, too, acknowledge. I hope I shall be able to show the hon. member that some of the proposals which he is advocating would have precisely the opposite effects from those he is seeking and, certainly, from those we on this side of the House are seeking-and here I speak as the minister responsible for the DREE program.
When I first entered the House of Commons I was, within a matter of days, assigned to the standing committee on transportation. Few who were members of the committee at that time are still in the House, though I can see one or two of them on each side of the House. I think
Transportation
they would agree with me that the fundamental issues we are debating today are not greatly different from those of nearly a decade ago. Many go back several decades, and some to the very beginnings of confederation.
It is interesting to note that the opposition, as well as individual critics outside the House, are suggesting that in some way or other it is these fundamental issues which have been creating problems. The implication is that, having existed for so long, they could in some magic way have been resolved between July 8, 1974, and March 10 of this year. Let me emphasize that I am referring to fundamental issues, not to day to day transportation problems which are bound to arise in a country as vast and as complex as Canada. Over the years we have been able to deal reasonably well with these problems, as any objective observer would agree. For example, to my personal knowledge, as one who was minister of transport for four years, transportation authorities from other countries are unanimous in agreeing that the over-all structure of transportation in Canada is one of the best in the world. Nevertheless, the fundamental issues remain, and by and large it is these which give rise to most of the criticism.
During the present debate I hope to put at least a few of these issues into perspective, and I hope hon. members will appreciate that in this context I am using the word "issue" as meaning a question about which there can be legitimate differences of opinion with important and valid interests ranged on opposite sides. I gave a good example of this when I referred to the position taken by the two speakers who preceded me. The real task is to recognize this interest to the maximum extent possible, and in many cases the methods of doing this have evaded governments of all political persuasions-federal, provincial and in some cases municipal. The various modes of transportation have not been able to resolve them and successive royal commissions, inquiries and regulatory agencies have been something less than wholly successful. What are the types of fundamental issues to which I have referred? I am not going to take the time to list all of them, but I will give a few examples without at this time coming down on the side of any particular interest group.
There is the long-standing issue referred to by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville, the Crowsnest pass rates, and a couple of larger problems, such as grain movement rationalization which involves both economic and social considerations and which, I am fully aware, is a highly emotional issue, as the hon. member has said, in terms of western Canada. But it also can be said that the Crowsnest pass issue and its related questions have bedevilled the development of rational, so-called developmental policies for perhaps as long as we have been a country, or at least as long as the western provinces have been in Canada.
In the east there is the Maritime Freight Rates Act and related subsidy programs. This is another fundamental issue. The appropriate level of tolls and long-term financing arrangements for the St. Lawrence Seaway is another. Then there is the difficult and continuing problem of determining with more precision what the role of various national carriers and agencies ought to be, how much autonomy they should enjoy and what their relationship
March 10, 1975

Transportation
should be to the government and to parliament. I propose to come back to some of these questions in a moment.
The same questions apply to Crown corporations and agencies and could be asked of federal-provincial relations as these relate to transportation, a field where there is divided, and sometimes fragmented, jurisdiction. Other fields where there are wide differences of opinion and of interest include ports administration, the type and size of merchant marine Canada ought to have, and shipping policy generally.
These few examples illustrate the complexity that surrounds Canada's transportation system; and I did not mention the air mode with the conflicting objectives of transcontinental or major carriers and the regionals. I could add the issue of the federal role in the operation of ferries, in the building and upgrading of highways and in coastal protection and services of various kinds. This is just a random sample and I am sure there are many important aspects of transportation which I have omitted in this brief review.
The essential point is that there is no unanimity on how these issues should be resolved; there is no unanimity on this basic question. Quite the contrary: anyone charged with formulating transportation policy-and here the Minister of Transport has my total sympathy, as he has the main responsibility in this regard-is inundated by conflicting views. The difficulty is, and this is a very key point I would ask members to note, that it is not simply a matter of separating sound opinion from the unsound; it lies in choosing between proposals that are frequently of equal validity but which are mutually exclusive.
Let me illustrate by dealing with the hardiest perennial of them all, freight rates, to which the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville gave a good deal of his time. Let me say at once that there continue to be anomalies and inequities in the freight rate structure that must be eliminated. Much has been done along these lines in recent years. If time permits, I will give certain examples because I do not think it is fair to blanket this issue and I do not think hon. members would want to be unfair by simply saying nothing has been done. A good deal has been done to eliminate certain anomalies, but even with further improvements we, as Canadians as well as legislators, will have to come to grips with certain basic questions. I suggest this in total sincerity, trying to put this matter into proper perspective.
It is my judgment that in most of the debates we have in this chamber, these questions tend to be ignored, perhaps because it is more immediate and more urgent to deal with some specific matter and perhaps, also, because it is easier to get one's mind around a specific matter than it is to come to grips with certain basic questions, which I shall attempt to do in the interest of generating what I hope will be a worth-while debate. For example, is the principle of compensatory rates valid? This principle is basic to the present National Transportation Act, but judging by the frequent comments of members in all parts of the House there are serious doubts on the issue. It is not enough to be opposed to the principle; it is necessary to decide what should be in its place if, in fact, it is going to be changed.
The record of the last seven or eight years makes it clear that this government has been prepared to make significant modifications to what was proposed and eventually

passed into law in the act of 1967. There has not been rigidity on the question of compensatory rates. There have been, for example, periodic freezes applied to certain categories of rates; substantial additional subsidies have been added under the MFRA and related legislation; the movement of various agricultural products, including feed grains, has been assisted at a cost of many millions of dollars; there have been increased subsidies for various types of coastal shipping, and the government has moved in directly to provide specialized rolling stock for the railways.
There are many other ways, also, in which the government has shown itself prepared to depart from the principle of compensatory rates. The argument persists, however, that there should be still more, even though the totality of demands one hears from all sides of the House-incidentally, not always from the opposition-is still on the basis of ad hockery and reflects no coherent plan. I find it difficult, and I hope I will be able to illustrate this as I go along, to rationalize the variety of proposals which come from members opposite, which in many respects, I suggest, if you look at them in isolation and then try to put them together into a package, are contradictory and not what the motion would call a cohesive and generally comprehensive transportation policy.
The reasons are perfectly clear and very understandable. Once a concession has been obtained, no beneficiary wishes to give it up. Therefore, the principle of compensatory rates becomes more and more distorted. Furthermore, there are grounds to question whether such individual measures designed to ease the impact of particular rates actually achieve their objectives. I want to re-emphasize that point if I may, Mr. Speaker, because I think it is important for us, when we are seeking ad hoc solutions which are very costly to the taxpayers of Canada, to ask ourselves whether in fact these individual measures are designed to ease the impact of particular rates and whether they achieve that objective.
Let us look at one example which bears on my responsibility to encourage regional development. When representatives of regions of the country away from the centre-that is most of Canada, in geographic terms; and I am sorry the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville is not here because this bears particularly on the remarks he made- complain about freight rates, it is often because such rates result in higher costs for goods which they purchase from central Canada. That is a very important point. Criticism of the rate structure may be entirely valid, but essentially that is the main basis for the complaint-that it costs more in various parts of the country to bring goods from central Canada.
I repeat that these complaints are understandable. If, however, there are substantial forms of assistance for traffic inbound to western Canada, eastern Canada or northern Canada, such assistance-I would ask members who make this point in Atlantic and western Canada to bear this in mind-really constitutes a subsidy to central Canadian manufacturers and shippers. It makes it harder for manufacturers in these areas, that is, the west and the east, to compete and in many cases it runs counter to the outbound subsidy programs the government has in place.
March 10, 1975

This is the reason I find it difficult, without hearing more detail on the question, to understand why the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville would suggest some equalling out of the freight rates structure all across the country. It seems to me that, clearly, would be counter-productive in terms of regional development initiative and what we are seeking to achieve. For example, all Atlantic provinces benefit from a 30 per cent subsidy on goods shipped out of the area. For certain value added commodities, the subsidy has been increased by my colleague the Minister of Transport-one of the many things he has done. It has been increased in recent years to 50 per cent. This subsidy is paid on truck as well as rail shipments. So 50 per cent of the total cost of moving certain goods out of the Altantic provinces is now subsidized.
Now, if Atlantic province manufacturers and processors, as well as certain primary producers, are to see their central Canada competitors subsidized to ship their goods into the eastern market, then the value of the subsidy, obviously, is reduced accordingly. What I am saying is that you cannot have it both ways in terms of subsidies. You cannot say in the Atlantic provinces or in western Canada that you want a break on the shipment of agricultural products to the centre, fisheries goods to the centre, or manufactured goods from both ends to the centre-that you want those subsidized-and at the same time ask for subsidies on goods moving from the centre to the outer perimeter of the country. It is clear that the same is true, as my friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) has said, of tariffs.
I should touch briefly on this matter once again because it is a good example of two worthy examples which can be self-defeating. In the first place we have consumers wanting to get their goods from whatever source at the lowest possible shipping cost, but every such concession can make it more difficult to achieve regional development. One of the most frequent complaints which I receive from western Canada relating to regional development concerns the freight rate on steel shipped from the east. In a broader context, the hon. member raised-as I am sure other members will, and I am sure the chief spokesman for the opposition is concerned about this-the question of so-called short haul rates versus long haul rates.
I agree with my colleague, the Minister of Transport, who has said on many occasions-as I have said in this House, and I am not altogether certain why some of these things should suddenly have new prominence because they are spoken by the present Minister of Transport, but perhaps I was not as effective as he in getting it across- that essentially the short haul-long haul differential is something with which this government has coped for many years and with which its predecessor government coped for many years. I should like to deal with it in steel terms, to start with, and then perhaps elaborate a little further.
On the question of steel, I concede readily that the arguments have merit in many cases, but my department is convinced that one of the major developmental opportunities that exists in western Canada centres on capacity in that region for a major steel producing facility. I do not think there is any doubt about that. I believe that more
Transportation
and more the examinations and discussions we are having with Alberta and Saskatchewan in particular tend to support this fact. Is it good policy? I ask the question, not rhetorically but in the interest of generating a worthwhile discussion on the question. Is it good policy, therefore, if the capability exists for further steel development in western Canada, to make it easier and less expensive for eastern steel manufacturers to penetrate the western market by an artificial lowering of rates, or should we in fact be encouraging, as we are, more steel making and thus a stronger economic base in the west?

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PRESENT CO-ORDINATED TRANSPORTATION POLICY

I shall be quite prepared to answer the question if there is time at the end, Mr. Speaker. There have been many conferences, and I have attended many discussions at which you begin with the premise that no short haul rates shall be higher than long haul rates, and then quickly you see it disintegrate in terms of any kind of consensus as you discover it bears differently upon different regions of western Canada. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the time of your comment I had given two examples of the complexity of a couple of regional development problems of major significance as they relate to transportation. I want to emphasize that neither of these examples is clear-cut. I do not suggest that I, or anyone else, have all the answers, recognizing that even within regions, trade and transportation issues compound the problem. For instance, it would not be sufficient to set up a steel freight rate from central Canada to western Canada and let it go at that. Our inquiries and studies indicate that if we are to have a major steel making capability in western Canada, this will require a very definite shift in the freight rate structure within the regions. This, I acknowledge and agree, is something that needs further examination.
Nevertheless, I suggest my basic point is valid. General freight rate freezes and blanket subsidies tend to work against regional development whatever benefit they may have to consumers. I might add that I have not been able to determine that many of the freight rate subsidy programs do in fact find their way to consumers, and here I speak particularly of the individual consumer. Consumers do not receive any significant benefit from them, so far as I have been able to determine. One has only to look at the recent study of consumer prices in the province of Newfoundland to see that transportation is by no means the main factor affecting consumer prices. Therefore, the concept that you can use transportation or freight rates specifically in order to reduce consumer costs is certainly open to question and should be examined thoroughly. It was determined that the distribution system within the province itself was a much more significant contribution to increased costs for consumers than the long distance transportation charges into the region.
In other words, once commodities get into the region, distribution services really need to be modernized and improved. I would expect this is true to the same extent in Atlantic Canada. This involves a good deal of private enterprise participation, which I do not rule out but which is certainly not the sole responsibility of the government.
Since time is short, I want to say a few brief words about another fundamental issue. I will be brief because of the limitation on time. I wish to speak about the toll system on the St. Lawrence Seaway. Here is another all-party effort, if you are talking about really fundamental issues on which decisions have to be made. It is significant that members of all parties from central and western Canada-it does not matter where these members happen to sit in the House-are strongly against any increase in Seaway tolls. In this, from my experience, they are accurately reflecting the views of their constituents.
At the same time, Atlantic province members-I include myself in this number-rarely, if ever, join in representations to keep tolls down on the St. Lawrence Seaway. In

this they, too, are echoing the views of those whom they represent, that the ports of Atlantic Canada suffer unfair competition from low Seaway tolls. Here, once again, we have another example of legitimate regional views being in conflict; and there are no easy answers. The government is being urged to cut costs, to behave in a businesslike manner; but if the logical steps were taken-I use the St. Lawrence Seaway simply as an example-in many of the other examples I have given, there would be greater inequities between regions and many national objectives would be thwarted.
In conclusion, I wish to touch briefly on one of the most difficult fundamental issues affecting Canadian transportation. It is the issue of jurisdiction, control and policymaking. A great deal has been made of the federal role in this regard, and of course no one quarrels with the key position that the federal government holds in this whole problem. I have spoken of a transportation system, in the singular. However, in reality we have dozens, even hundreds, of different and often competing components within that system. Not all of these are subject to federal control, and where there is federal responsibility it is exercised in a variety of ways.
I would invite hon. members to examine this structure. It is not this government, or any particular government, but parliament itself which has frequently reaffirmed its belief that Crown corporations must continue to enjoy a high degree of autonomy. I have no quarrel with that view, and certainly many instances have been brought forward in this House where indeed there have been claims that the government has been interfering too much with Crown corporations. There is, however, an inconsistency in the view often taken by members-again, I am not referring to any particular party-that the government should direct CNR or Air Canada, for example, to follow a particular course of action. Having said that, I repeat what I said at the outset, namely, that the role of Crown corporations, especially in the transportation field, is something that generates a great deal of heated debate with many valid arguments on both sides.
Harking back to the first comments that were made this afternoon regarding the nationalization of CPR, any kind of rationalization that would be massive in scope and would change drastically the long-established precedents for the relationship between Crown corporations, the government and parliament would be hotly debated and there would be no unanimity of view in the House on that important subject.
The same can be said of the Canadian Transport Commission. Parliament has given the commission certain wide-ranging powers, and it did so deliberately. I was here at the time as a member of the committee and I am sure that others who were there at the time-I do not want to single anyone out-would be prepared to confirm that it was done deliberately to cut down on the degree of direct government intervention. That was deemed to be a wise course at that particular time. Once again, this may be a highly commendable objective. The government or the responsible minister cannot be faulted for observing the law and allowing the processes set out in the act to be followed. If there is to be a change in the CTC approach and in the responsibility that it has, then parliament itself
March 10, 1975

will have to decide whether it wishes the government to become more directly involved. Indeed, this is a question, I repeat, on which there is no unanimity of opinion and which, I hope hon. members will appreciate, makes the job of any Minister of Transport exceedingly difficult.
There is another important aspect of jurisdiction, and that is the authority of the provinces, particularly in the matter of highway regulations and similar matters. While there are undoubted federal responsibilities in this field, the jurisdiction is shared, at the very least. Incidentally, it is interesting to note the history of federal responsibility in this field. It was on the basis of a 1956 Supreme Court judgment in the long run, and not so much because of any desire on the part of the federal government to be deeply involved in highway management or trucking, that the federal government was brought into the field. Therefore, there is no way to proceed other than through agreement and consensus, which are sometimes difficult to achieve.
The federal government, and particularly my own department, is helping many provinces to upgrade their road systems and to achieve certain national standards. Many millions of federal dollars will be spent on this objective again this year in the east, and also through the efforts of the Minister of Transport in consultation with western provinces to do upgrading on certain key network roads in western Canada. This will be an ongoing expenditure.
It is interesting to note that if one takes the average year since the end of construction of the TransCanada Highway, despite the fact that the primary responsibility is with the provinces the federal government in one way or another has contributed, on average, something like $190 million a year to road building in this country, a significant and important sum in terms of what it has been able to achieve. As we get better standards, in highway terms, across the country, a consensus is more likely to emerge in terms of provinces. But one should not underestimate a good deal of the anxiety that the provinces have about yielding any more than they have to of provincial jurisdiction or authority in this field. In this, frequently they are aided and abetted, for its particular reasons, by the trucking industry.
My objective today was to show in a realistic fashion some of the very real complexities that exist within the Canadian transportation framework. It is these to which the Minister of Transport refers when he discusses, with his usual candour as the hon. member has said, the difficulties involved both in policy-making and in keeping such a huge system operational. The difficulties are not new; they are not the creation of any one government or of any one period. They will not be solved by criticism alone, or by simply pointing out the flaws in the system, which everybody concedes continue to exist even after 100 years. They will not be solved by criticism, although frankly I consider constructive debate to be useful. If there is a debate in which suggestions can be made of specific ways in which transportation can be used to better advantage to aid regional development, then I want to hear those suggestions regardless of the quarter of the House from which they come.
What we must do, and what a great many others outside parliament must do, is to make some choices, because this
Transportation
is not a problem that can be resolved purely by legislation or co-operation between different levels of government; there are enormous private industry factors here which have to be part of the over-all exercise. Incidentally, perhaps a national conference might not be a bad idea, and I am sure the Minister of Transport would accept it as a worth-while suggestion.
It seems to me that if there is a great weakness-and perhaps I should plead guilty to part of that weakness, having been the responsible minister for some time-it is that in transportation, when it comes to the crunch, it is frequently easier and, perhaps one could say frankly, in the national interest to achieve some kind of accommodation that falls short of perfection rather than try abruptly to remove from the various elements in the transportation system some key element to which a particular region or interest group is very strongly dedicated.
So I say that we must make some choices if we are to get the cohesive policy to which reference is made today in the motion of the opposition. None of this will be easy, and on the fundamental issues which I have outlined there will be wide differences: I am sure that the same will be true of others I have not touched on because of time limitations.
If all hon. members go about this task in a reasonable, orderly way which gets to the root of the problem, and if they are prepared to face up to these root problems, whether they live in the east or the west, and examine some of the issues I have outlined, I do not suggest we will find all the answers: that may be too much to expect and, quite frankly, in a rapidly changing field like transportation I have no doubt that it will be difficult to achieve perfection. Nevertheless, we will continue to make what I think we have made over the years, and certainly over the years of this government, namely, progress.
