speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Friday last on March 7, a motion of the Progressive Conservatives questioned the ability of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) to organize and develop a sure, efficient, coordinated modern transport system on par with the needs of national and regional economies, external trade and social welfare in Canada, in accordance with the undertakings made in the Speech from the Throne. And now today, Mr. Speaker, motion No. 15 introduced by the Progressive Conservative party condemns the government's failure to present a co-ordinated transportation policy.
Mr. Speaker, I hope that the Minister of Transport will have heard enough about transport problems since Friday to retain his attention. However, since I have been sitting in Parliament, I denounced on many occasions this lack of co-ordination in transport generally and more especially in our railway system.
This is not a new problem, Madam Speaker, since it has existed under both governments, which seem to take pleasure in accusing each other and rejecting the blame on each other.

March 10, 1975
Transportation
Last Friday, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) was telling the Progressive Conservatives: You did not do better than us in the past; you are always criticizing, but make concrete proposals, tell us what is your policy, tell us what to do, and we shall act. This is the behaviour of a government which was so strong, which said that it was strong and capable of the greatest things during the whole election campaign and is now weak and powerless when it is in power. The government is suddenly so devoid of ideas that it must beg the opposition for some answers. In his speech of March 7, 1975, last Friday, as is reported on page 3894 of Hansard, the Minister of Transport, when he realized that his appeal was falling into deaf ears continued his speech by saying, and I quote:
The only answer I get from the opposition is: It takes a long time! But, Mr. Speaker, should I, as Minister of Transport, be quicker about changing the whole transportation system in Canada than the Conservatives about designating a new leader?
This is how the minister clowns to get rid of a serious problem which is of great concern for all Canadians. I sincerely ask you what the replacement of the Progressive Conservative leader has to do with the transport situation. Mr. Speaker, I ask the Minister of Transport to be a bit more serious, and I know that he can do so when he is clear-minded in the House. The minister must realize once and for all that the election campaign is over, that we are here to find answers to the problems, and that it is up to the government to propose solutions to the House since generally all the legislation to be voted is introduced by the government.
I am in favour of this motion, and I hope that the government will not consider it simply as an insignificant criticism, but as a pressing appeal from the Canadian people to work concretely to solve the big and thorny problem of transportation across Canada. Be it transportation by water, by air or by land, I am sure we have everything that is needed to provide Canadians with an adequate and well coordinated transportation system.
Last week, we discussed our ridiculous situation with regard to the nonexistent merchant marine in Canada. On Friday, many members referred to our air transportation system, which is far from being adapted to our needs. In my region, at least, we have no congratulations to extend to the present minister and even less to all the other ministers who preceded him.
During the last six election campaigns, Madam Speaker, we received in my riding of Roberval dozens of ministers who gave rise to the highest expectations among the people. The Minister of Finance himself (Mr. Turner) came and promised on his honour of gentleman that if his government were reelected, he would order the complete rebuilding of the Roberval airport. Let us see what we "salvaged" from the visit of that flight of doves?
I ask him again today: where is his honour of gentleman, and why did he come and give false hopes to our people? I ask the present Minister of Transport who, at the time Minister for Regional Economic Expansion, had $500 million to distribute as productively as possible electorally, what has happened to all those beautiful promises for an airport at Dolbeau and Saint-Felicien? At the time he said an airport was needed at almost every centre in my riding to meet the demand. What has he done since? And particu-

larly, what will he do now that he is a full-fledged minister? We are still waiting.
I cannot miss this wonderful opportunity of speaking once again to the minister about the problems we have been running up against for years with regard to the Canadian National, since it is the only Crown company in our area.
First, let us speak of the freight service. After ten years of requests, has the problem of freight cars been solved? Here is some correspondence, Madam Speaker, that speaks for itself. This letter is dated February 21, 1974; it is addressed to the Minister of Transport. It comes from the Domtar Company. I quote:
The problem of the shortage of railway cars for the transport of newsprint, pulp and shavings seems to be widespread.
A few of the fifty-six pulp and paper industries in the province of Quebec depend almost entirely on railways for the movement of freight, to and from their facilities. The remaining ones, while having access to other modes, still count on rail to a large extent for their incoming and outcoming trade. Although the size of the shipments involved cannot be determined exactly, since they include raw materials and finished products, we know very well that the volume and revenues of such movements by rail are very high indeed. In any event, adequate rail service is one factor in the maintaining and economy of production of these plants.
For more than a year, railway cars have not been available in sufficient numbers. The problem is aptly summed up in the following remarks by one freight movement officer: "The availability of freight cars is a day-to-day affair; there are never enough cars to meet the demand, and we must constantly pressure railways to get our share of available rolling stock".
There is a serious scarcity of cars for newsprint. Very often the type of car required cannot be obtained. The use of another type of car entails higher costs, since it is impossible to load the specified minimum into shorter cars, with the result that we must pay freight on dead weight. The lack of cars when needed forces companeis to store their products and rehandle them, at extra cost. Some companies have to use trucks to compensate for inadequate rail service. One major company indicated the loss of sales by reason of a persisting scarcity of cars. As far as the movement of chips is concerned, substitution of boxcars for the usual gondola cars creates difficulties, as well as needless costs caused by dead weight; because at certain times, loadings are below minimum ...
Time is lacking to read the whole letter through, but this proves to the department that the companies constantly requested more adequate and more cars, without avail.
Let us now talk about our famous passenger service. On April 17, 1973, I pointed out to the Minister of Transport the need for an immediate improvement in passenger services. There was at that time an outbreak of derailments that were attributed to all kinds of causes, without the real one ever being denounced. There were even wild accusations that train engineers had shortened the allowed time for a haul by half an hour. Let us not forget that on our local circuit speed should not exceed 25 or 30 miles an hour. I am sure that Montreal or Ottawa travellers would not want to hear about trains anymore if they travelled at such speed.
Are the railway tracks between Montreal, Chambord and Dolbeau too weak? Let us go and watch freight trains more than 100 cars long roll by. Incidentally, we have always exposed the lack of maintenance as the great evil.
March 10, 1975

Teams of three or four men are designated when those teams should be made of six or even eight men.
That is the first mistake technoracts in Montreal offices make when they perhaps never went on a field check. When I say field check I do not mean spend five or ten minutes in brain centre offices before returning to Montreal with their report. I mean they should run the track with maintenance attendants. That way, Madam Speaker, we could get much better results.
If CNR decided one day to play its role which is to give good service, its clientele the heads of that Crown corporation should stop thinking that hotels are their first priority in that system of transportation. Those people forget entirely that if they want to ensure a good clientele for hotels, here again, a good and well coordinated system of transportation will enable them to achieve it.
It CNR wants a profitable passenger service, it must first provide an adequate service with planned schedules and well maintained cars. It seems quite strange to talk about those matters, Madam Speaker, but in my area I think the directors of that corporation have completely lost sight of the basic principles, with the result that fewer and fewer people want to use CNR services.
On several occasions we showed that the Chambord-Montreal passenger run could be done in five hours, while it now takes eight or ten hours, if there is no delay. I would say incidently that delay is the trademark of CNR in our area. The cause of that slowness is that at present freight has priority. Consequently, we must wait hours along the route to allow freight to run freely. That is ridiculous, one might say, but it is the simple truth.
I shall just take the example of the Montreal bound train which leaves Chambord on Sunday night. In spite of all the useless delays, it reaches Montreal by 7 a.m., so that we can take any other train to Toronto, Ottawa or elsewhere. But if you happen to take the very same train any week day, you have to wait for the train from Abitibi, which is always very late. And so you reach Montreal by 10 or 11 a.m., and even frequently after 12 noon.
We have been wondering for years why it should not be an all-Sunday week for the CN in our area. The Sunday night train might very easily take two hours less if the authorities would give Montreal bound passenger trains priority. We also suggested the implementation of a direct daytime service to Montreal.
Madam Speaker, may I call it five o'clock?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, this debate which occurs at a very appropriate time is indicative of the inability and inconsciousness of the government regarding transportation. We are obligated to the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) for having submitted to the attention of the House the motion we are now studying, which faithfully reflects not only the concern of the official opposition, but also that of all Canadian citizens about the complete and permanent disorder existing in the Department of Transport.
It is obvious, Madam Speaker, when considering the government's performance in this field, one would be tempted to say as in the song: "Faut-il en rire ou faut-il en pleurer?" But when considering the minister's accomplishments, I fear there is no alternative but to pity him. This is what leads me to adopt towards him perhaps a more sympathetic attitude than would justify the mess his department is in, sympathetic because I had hoped that before this debate or perhaps during the first day on Friday last the minister would find a way to answer the members' concerns and set forth the solutions he wants to bring in, indicate a general policy, the new policy he intends to advocate in transport.
However, to our great disappointment, the minister rather took delight in falling back on means which in the art of oratory have certainly their merits but are not acceptable on the Parliamentary level. That is how, Madam Speaker, I have considered the minister who, noticeably disturbed, irritated by the questions put to him for some time on account of this mess existing within his department, and under pressure about this issue of the Hamilton and lie d'Orleans dredging contracts, the Minister of Transport, in my opinion one of the most pathetic ministers in Canadian history-I am saying this almost with a measure of friendship-had to raise his voice in the House last Friday. And over the weekend, Madam Speaker, the papers printed the following headlines:
"Marchand Alleged Victim of Racist Campaign"
"Marchand blows his top and is blown up".
"Marchand notes evidence of suspicion and racism".
"Accused of incompetency, Marchand seeks an end to racist attacks". "Strong attack by Marchand against English-speaking racists' aspersion casting".
March 10, 1975

Transportation
Last weekend, Madam Speaker, these media reported to the Canadian public the statements the minister made and which he will not withdraw, judging from what I have just heard, statements he made both in the House and outside to the reporters of French-speaking press. In all fairness to and out of regard for him, I refer him to this statement he made to the French-speaking press and I quote:
"I have been living here since 1965, and I have witnessed the Lamontagne affair, the Favreau affair and the Tremblay affair. Wherever there were French Canadians, they attacked them. And who are they attacking in the House now? The Minister of Transport, Jean Chretien, Yves Pratte. If you look up the oral question period for the past month, you will see that this is what is going on."
This last remark was made by the Minister of Transport, as though his outburst had not been enough, and as though he needed hidden threats, he added:
"And if they want to play this little game, we are going to play it rough".
Madam Speaker, I wanted to report those remarks, to note the minister's attitude and behaviour, in order that he knew how essential it is for Parliament that a Crown minister act with objectivity and impartiality, and foremost how essential that he was not too sensitive about some criticisms and that he never thought that when a minister's competence is questioned, his race, his colour or his origins are attacked.

Madam Speaker, it is not surprising that when the issue of the minister's competence is raised, when the issue of the minister's admitted transportation mess is raised, the minister claims that my colleagues are making prejudicial and racial attacks on him personally. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) and his now well known consensus have been attacked by members on this side of the House of both English and French background, yet he does not feel personally slighted or racially attacked.
The Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) has been attacked at times for lack of direction, and for a basic sloppiness of approach, by myself and others, yet he does not feel particularly slighted or racially offended. If we attack a minister who happens to be of French Canadian origin, according to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) we do so for racial or prejudicial reasons. When we attack a minister of English Canadian origin, according to the Minister of Transport we do so to divide English from French in this country's government.
While paranoia expressed consistently in an emotional fashion either inside or outside this House does not constitute a direct infringement on the privileges of members, surely the House can understand that the workings of government and the processes of this House are not aided by the type of shrill accusations and meanderings of the Minister of Transport. Surely, Madam Speaker, compared to his cabinet colleagues he has little to be worried about. The Minister of Finance must have at least every second taxpayer in this country after him. The Minister of National Defence (Mr. Richardson) has a steadily diminishing but nevertheless 80,000 loyal and well armed defence forces upset with him. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has taken on all of Canada's consumers and, despite a basic kinship with the fertilizer producers, he

has them to worry about as well. The Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) must have to hire people to open his mail. The Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) has thousands of unemployed speech writers trying to break down his door-

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I want to concentrate on one vital aspect of transportation policy in Canada this afternoon, namely, regional air policy. Unfortunately, discussion on this subject has been sidetracked by the introduction of extraneous matters by the minister, so I want to get back on target this afternoon by zeroing in on a specific problem.
The speaker who just preceded me referred to the Hon. Lionel Chevrier as an outstanding leader in the development of transportation policy in Canada. I had a conversation recently with Mr. Chevrier in his capacity as President of Nordair. I can assure the hon. member that he was less than happy concerning the direction regional air policy has been taking during recent months.
I have some sympathy for the minister and the problems that confront him so I am not going to personalize my remarks this afternoon by zeroing in on any particular minister. The problems that have been outlined effectively by opposition spokesmen are the by-product of several recent ministers.
I was interested this afternoon to hear the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) take part in the debate. He was a former Minister of Transport. In fact, he changed places with the present incumbent in that position. I listened to the minister in charge of DREE and suspected that he was preaching for a call, as though he would like to get back on the job as Minister of Transport.
There was a little bit of uncertainty as to who was going to be the major spokesman this afternoon in replying to the presentation of opposition members, and it will be interesting to see the permutations of any Cabinet shuffle, as they unfold in the weeks that lie ahead, particularly if there is to be a transfer of responsibility in this portfolio.
March 10, 1975

The major difficulty in transportation policy arises from the failure of the government to come to grips with the MacPherson Report, which in the early 1960's resulted from an examination in detail of transportation problems in this country. After several years' delay, following the change of government in 1963, a new transportation policy was finally forthcoming. It established the Canadian Transport Commission in place of the old Board of Transport Commissioners. Placed in charge of the CTC was a former minister of transport, who has been referred to from time to time in this Chamber. In fact, during the question period today we had a very interesting question answered in respect of the position of that former minister of transport, the Hon. Jack Pickersgill, who shifted sideways from a ministerial responsibility to the chairmanship of the CTC. Incidentally he was followed by another former minister of the government.
In 1972 the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Stanfield) made the specific promise that should he become leader of the government in Canada this business of shifting ministers of transport and other former ministers of the Crown to head important bodies like the CTC would end forthwith. The tendency is to politicize those bodies which should above all else have an independent expertise in respect of transportation problems.
One of the major reasons we are in the mess that has been described by the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) as "a mess that is worse than anyone realizes" is that we have not had the leadership from the body designated by this parliament to bring the required expertise into the resolution of the extremely complex problems of transportation, recognized by everyone in this House.

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PRESENT CO-ORDINATED TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Because it is a political graveyard it has also become the graveyard of all the fine hopes expressed in the MacPherson Report, which ushered in the legislation establishing the CTC with the hope of bringing order out of existing confusion.
To get back to the specific problem, the failure to move forward on a rational regional air policy, I point out that in 1973 the present minister announced route divisions between Air Canada and CP Air as designated international flag carriers for Canada. That was a good and positive step, and we applauded the minister for his initiative. He announced also that there would be two further announcements to deal with the fundamental problems involved in regional air policy, plus a supplementary statement on third level air carriers which would fill the gap in existing air transportation policy.
Some two years later we have not moved beyond the original initiative of the minister. As a result, general air policy and third level carrier policy have been a matter of flying by the seat of the pants on the part of the minister and the government. There is no guidance, no direction, and no policy which makes it possible for the five designated regional carriers to plan on a long-term basis.

speechtext:
I am coming to that in a moment, and I will not be sidetracked at this stage of my remarks.
The tragedy in respect of regional development is that air policy, as it has been designed to the moment, is geared to the needs of Air Canada, and I think this can be easily demonstrated by some of the recent decisions in respect of regional air policy. I cannot go into too much detail, but the application by Nordair to provide a service between Thunder Bay, Sudbury, Ottawa and Montreal was rejected. This is where the Hon. Lionel Chevrier quarrels with the present lack of policy. Air Canada expressed no interest in that route, but as soon as Nordair submitted its application Air Canada submitted an application and Air Canada was given the right to provide that particular segment of regional air service.
At every opportunity this minister comes to the defence of the monopoly position of Air Canada, as he did in the House the other day when the hon. member for Vegreville (Mr. Mazankowski) asked for a copy of the Air Canada contract, which was formerly called a contract between the government of Canada and Trans-Canada Airlines. The reply by the minister was that to reveal this information would do irreparable harm to Air Canada. We have now discovered that the information is available in the National Archives of Canada.
It has become the case that whatever Air Canada wants, it is that which determines what the Cabinet decides. That is why Nordair has decided to appeal the decision of the Air Transport Committee, with every right, because Nordair was operating under the designated regional policy laid down by the former minister in 1966, and extended as recently as 1973.
Now I should like to move to the specific problem to which the minister has already referred as it applies to Manitoba and Saskatchewan. For over a year now the western part of Manitoba and the eastern part of Saskatchewan have had no air service whatsoever. This situation has existed in spite of the fact that the minister said that adequate air service is absolutely essential for regional economic development. He was supported in this statement by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion when he spoke this afternoon.
In order to help us understand how this situation of a complete vacuum and void in prairie air transportation policy has developed I have in front of me the regional air carriers' latest information booklet in which they show the routes that are already covered by the regional air carriers in Canada. The province of Saskatchewan has absolutely no regional air service whatsoever, and west of Winnipeg Transair is not carrying out its responsibility. This again is related to the basic broad orientation of the minister that what is good for Air Canada is good for everybody else.
Let me give a little history. Air Canada originally accepted the responsibility to provide the service. It provided an excellent service right through from Calgary to Winnipeg. With the announcement of the regional policy in 1966 Air Canada asked to be relieved of this responsibility and to have it turned over to the designated regional carrier, Transair. Because that run was not economically

feasible a subsidy was provided. Let me talk about this business of the subsidy.
Because there are very few air services in the smaller communities which actually pay for themselves it is essential that such services be subsidized from the national treasury. If the subsidy had been continued it would be a lot less expensive than the program of the commuter air service which is about to be launched. This service will not involve a regional air carrier but will involve a third level carrier even though we have not yet had a policy for third level carriers enunciated by the minister.
As an indication that the government had long term plans, runways were strengthened and lengthened. In 1970 the new terminal at Brandon was opened and it was such an auspicious occasion that the Minister of Transport at that time, the present Minister of Regional Economic Expansion, attended in person the terminal opening and made marvellous forecasts of how the service would be expanded in the future. Since then everything has been downhill. The subsidy was withdrawn and the service was downgraded to commuter third level service provided by Midwest Airlines, a subsidiary of Transair. Since January a year ago there has been no service.
It was the Air Transport Committee that gave permission to stop the air service into that area over a year ago. I shall deal with this in a moment in relation to a decision which that committee brought down with reference to an application Transair had before that committee for a year, in which it offered to meet its obligation to the regional air policy and to provide a first-class jet service between Prince Albert, Regina, Brandon and Toronto, without subsidy.
In giving a negative decision on the jet application, the Air Transport Committee obviously was looking over its shoulder, because on page 11 of its decision it states:
The concerns of the Saskatchewan government and the Regina Chamber of Commerce stem in part from the intervention of Air Canada respecting the adverse effect of the Transair proposal on Air Canada traffic and hence on its future plans for improved service.
In other words the committee was aware of the fact that if this were done Air Canada would not improve the service as it had intended. In its decision the committee states:
The committee is sympathetic to the concern expressed by Brandon and the communities in the Brandon area that the citizens of that area have to travel via surface to Winnipeg in order that they may connect with flights of a mainline or regional nature. The committee wishes to point out, had Transair or any other applicant made application to serve Brandon in a different manner than Transair has in this application, and, in addition justified the need for such a service, the committee would have given serious consideration to such an application.
In other words the decision of the committee was based on the attitude that Air Canada takes to these important matters. I want to suggest to the minister, who has referred to this third level commuter service, that it will not serve any useful purpose unless it is linked to a regional first-class service which makes it possible for Transair to discharge its obligation west of Winnipeg. I am sure the minister will agree that it is quite unreasonable and out of context with regional air policy to have Transair and its service at Winnipeg. It flies between Winnipeg, Dryden, Thunder Bay and Toronto, but does not provide any service west of Winnipeg because the ACT

has refused to authorize the provision of service in that area of responsibility.
I wish to make some precise suggestions before my time expires, whereby the minister can enhance his reputation and deal with a specific problem. I have been in correspondence with his former parliamentary secretary, the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay). I received this reply in a letter signed by the deputy minister, Mr. Stoner:
Under the Aeronautics Act, applications for licences to operate commercial air services are made to the Canadian Transport Commission, and the Commission, not the Minister, may issue the licence. However, under the National Transportation Act an appeal from a decision of the Commission on an application for a licence under the Aeronautics Act is provided to the Minister. It would hardly then be proper for the Minister to interfere with a decision of the Commission in the first instance or to express his opinion on a matter before the Committee which might later be the subject of an appeal to him.
I ask the minister to accept his responsibility under the Transportation Act and appeal the decision of the committee, since it seems that this is the only way we will ever have adequate air service under the regional air policy. I would hope a public hearing would be held in this regard. The decision of the committee was brought down after a delay of more than a 12 months' period, and there were no public hearings. As is indicated by the decision from which I quoted, the ATC was sympathetic to the application in the realization that the air service was inadequate in the context of regional air policy. I believe the commission would have been willing to acquiesce, but because there was opposition by Air Canada to the effect that it interfered with its monopoly position in that part of western Manitoba and eastern Saskatchewan, the proposition was turned down.
I would hope also that the minister would meet with the regional air carriers. The regional air carriers obviously are quite concerned about the present policy. I trust that the minister has read the booklet which outlines their concerns. Perhaps I can best draw his attention to the situation by reading from the booklet itself. It refers to the fact that the policy was laid down in 1966. It states:
They were to provide regular route operations into the North, and to operate local and regional routes to complement the main carriers.
... The government also proposed a modest subsidy policy to aid the development of marginal air routes.
It refers to the fact that in 1969 there was a refinement of government policy which divided the country into regions covered by the five present regional carriers. With reference to Transair, the prairie provinces and northwestern Ontario were the designated area of responsibility for this regional carrier. A little note is added here that later Transair was also given access to Toronto. I ask the minister: why does that responsibility end at Winnipeg? Why is it not extended to cover such areas as Brandon, Regina and Prince Albert? Transair had to withdraw from this obligation because of the withdrawal of the subsidy.
The minister has indicated that a third level carrier is about to be established. The government's participation in this third level carrier operation is to provide two aircraft. There is no operating subsidy. The provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan have had difficulties meeting the obligations governing the operation subsidy.

In conclusion, Madam Speaker, I ask the minister to compare this with STOL for which the government has taken complete financial responsibility. It is a demonstration project. The same designation is given to the proposed commuter service between Yorkton, Dauphin, Brandon and Winnipeg. Let us be fair and equitable, and let us take a thorough look at the proposition that has been put forward by Transair and turned down. Will the minister use the authority that is granted him under the legislation to ask for a review, and particularly refer the matter to the people?

speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I see there are a few minutes remaining before six o'clock. I am very pleased to be able to intervene in this debate as a mere, humble backbencher. I have been here six or seven months, and I find that whenever the subject of transportation comes up for discussion in the House it is always discussed in terms of freight rates or the regional air policy, such as was referred to by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale). Regional matters are very important, and it appears to me that parliament does not hear too often the voice from central Canada on intercity rail, for example.
Let me state briefly the problem of intercity rail transportation in the context of this debate. One thing we must remember is that the issue is very complex. I think that my colleague, the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson), summed it up very well when he castigated the opposition for expecting a well defined transportation policy to be enunciated, introduced to parliament, and to become law in the space of a few months. This is not possible.
A debate on transport has been going on now for two days, and I think that my intervention this afternoon contains the first mention of intercity rail transport. It is a very wide subject indeed. I will refer to the words of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) when he spoke on Friday and said that we must find the best techniques to ensure the best possible service for Canadians. We should not try to rush off and implement a new policy just because the opposition members are getting hot under the collar and are prodding us every which way. To prepare a new policy takes time.
On Friday, the hon. member for Burnaby-Richmond-Delta (Mr. Reynolds)-who was here a few minutes ago and who is now lurking behind the curtains-referred to our party's well received transportation policy in the last election campaign. He said that it was enunciated but that no legislation had come before the House as yet. He knows as well as I do that many of our proposals do not require new legislation. As I shall show later, the minister is leading the way in implementing these new policies. In fact I might say as an aside that one of the things that made me proud to stand as a Liberal candidate in the last federal election representing an urban constituency in Toronto was the party's transportation policy.

Transportation
in the last election campaign were good ones, and that many salient points were brought out for the benefit of all Canadians.
One of our proposals last summer was for the establishment of a Canadian Passenger Transport Corporation to assume responsibility for the operation of all intercity passenger train services which are now the responsibility of CNR and CPR. The government in a sense issued a warning to the railways, through this proposed policy for the establishment of a corporation, to start paying attention to rail passenger services, especially in the high density traffic corridor between Windsor and Quebec, and to pay attention to passenger needs between Montreal, Ottawa, Toronto, southwestern Ontario, the Atlantic provinces and the links between Edmonton and Calgary.
This proposal was bold and had the effect of creating- to use President Theodore Roosevelt's words from a by-gone era-"a big stick," because it appears, from all I read, from my travels on CNR these days, and from the remarks I heard from the president of CPR, that the railways are getting the message and are making a conscientious effort to upgrade their services. We have now the Turbo train running twice daily between Montreal and Toronto. I believe it runs once a day between Ottawa and Montreal. On Friday night, due to the disruption in the air service, my colleague, the hon. member for Middlesex-London-Lambton (Mr. Condon), and I travelled six and a half hours on that great CN train to Toronto. I think we were very well looked after, except for the speed at which the train travelled, something to which I will make reference in a moment. In any event we had a very comfortable ride!
It is clear that speed is essential in rail travel, but that the railways at present cannot achieve it. However, with the assistance of this government they will be able to achieve it. Before the hour of six o'clock I was talking about the need for speed in intercity rail travel, and I put forth the argument that the railways really will have difficulty in matching our expectations unless the government comes forward with some assistance in helping to develop new technology, such as the very successful light, rapid, comfortable rail cars now being tested. Indeed, I believe the LRC test locomotive is being used on the daily Tempo run from Toronto to Sarnia pulling conventional coaches. These trains can attain speeds of up to 125 miles per hour.

The test with the LRC is essentially designed to allow railway personnel to become familiar with the operation of a daily service and to see how the equipment performs in an endurance sense over a certain period. Recently the LRC completed thousands of miles of testing at the Am track Centre in the United States.
There are other ways in which the government can be of assistance in the development of intercity rail transport. We must remember that there are massive capital outlays required to build a new double track paralleling the present CN right of way from Montreal to Toronto. The government can assist in funding a fully computerized signalling system on the railways, concrete ties, electrification, and continuously welded track. All of these will help facilitate a high speed rail system. I understand that discussions are now under way with CN to look into some of these possibilities. In fact I was informed that only last Friday, the day when this debate began, that the Minister of Transport met with senior officials from both Canadian National and Canadian Pacific to discuss ways of improving intercity rail passenger services.
As for Canadian Pacific, the big stick of the Canadian Passenger Transport Corporation proposal to which I referred earlier in my remarks, I am sure prompted Mr. Sinclair, the president of Canadian Pacific, in his recent remarks to admit that existing technology would permit CP to introduce highspeed rail links on the Montreal-Ottawa line and to cut down the travel time to about 75 minutes; and I reiterate to my hon. friend from Burnaby-Richmond-Delta, who is not here at the present time, that no new legislation is needed in this case, only the good will and the determination of the railways to comply with government intentions. The failure to comply with what we believe on this side of the House is the direction in which intercity rail should go would leave the government in a very dicey position. There is one alternative left if we do not receive the co-operation of the railways, and that is the full nationalization of the rail section of CP and the creation of one Canadian railway company, publicly owned, and serving the interests of Canada.
Hon. members of the Official Opposition this afternoon sneered when this solution was proposed by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom), but it is the responsibility of the government to see that Canada's railway companies, which receive so much in the way of massive financial assistance from the taxpayers of Canada in the form of bonds, debentures, loans, land grants, etc., serve the present needs of the Canadian population.
The revitalization of our passenger rail services will involve a vast construction program for public transport vehicles and thus create an enormous area of industrial employment opportunity. I understand that there are now about 800,000 Canadians already employed in the transportation field alone, and this will be vastly increased by revamping the rolling stock through the introduction of new types of railway cars such as the LRCs. Revitalization of our intercity rail systems with high speed trains will help to decentralize growth in our urban areas. As a member for the metropolitan Toronto region I am very concerned about this particular facet of intercity rail.
Intercity rail development will help to add stimuli to smaller communities by offering them a fast direct link to

major metropolises. It will help them become small industrial centres. It will help them become bedroom communities for the larger centres. It will for the first time create competition for the airlines in many domestic shorthaul routes-shorthaul routes which wastefully consume jet fuel in an age of scarcity, crowd air terminals and exacerbate the noise problem for thousands of residents in the urban areas, especially in the west end of Toronto. Perhaps those of us who took a stand on this side of the House in doubting somewhat the wisdom of the government going ahead with the building of a second airport in the Pickering area will be justified in the end as a highspeed rail system could dampen demand for air transport in the dense corridor between Quebec and Windsor.
I would like to digress for just a moment to refer to the minister and his approach to the Pickering airport and the needs of that area. It is no secret that there was much discussion on this side of the House. There was much internal debate and opposition to the proposed full scale $1.5 billion Pickering Airport; but it is the measure of the present minister, who has suffered from the spurious and vituperative attacks of hon. members on the other side of this House, that he listened to hon. members on this side, took their counsel, and agreed after much deliberation to scale down the size of that airport. It is now a $250 million proposal. There is the option to expand if those critics of the airport are wrong, but I believe it leaves the door open to develop new ways of transporting people in the high density corridor along the Lake Ontario-St. Lawrence region.
I could go on to talk about the spinoffs of a highspeed rail system as it will affect our urban areas, such as weekend excursions for winter weekends for workers in cities, or to take masses of city dwellers to the lakeside in the heat of the summer, but I think I should conclude because I know there are other speakers who wish to contribute this evening.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) will be happy to know that I do not plan to speak very long on this motion. I would not want the minister to think that I am picking on him just because I think that he should have come up with a transport policy of some kind during the years that he has had his portfolio. After all, if a member accepts a portfolio, such as the Minister of Transport has, we in the opposition and the Canadian people as well, have a right to expect him to tell us from time to time what are his policies. If he does not have any policies then he can expect to have the opposition keep the pressure on until he comes up with some.
My own interest, strangely enough, Mr. Speaker, has to do with rail service, or the lack of rail service, in my riding of Parry Sound-Muskoka, and in many parts of Canada such as western and northern Ontario. I know most people think of Parry Sound-Muskoka as a little corner of Paradise, or the Garden of Eden, and naturally think that it is off the beaten path, off the main line, so to speak. But that just is not so, Mr. Speaker. My riding is on the main line to Sudbury and North Bay, and for that reason you would think that it would be easy for the railways to provide adequate rail service through it.
There are a number of reasons why the people of Parry Sound-Muskoka have a right to expect the railroads to serve them, or at least to pretend once in a while that they know that we exist. The minister could show from one of his old timetables, that we used to have fairly regular rail service, passenger and freight, through my riding, and he could add that the people did not take advantage of the service and so it was cut off. The fact is that the regular service that we used to have came through at such times as to make it inconvenient, if not impossible, for people to take advantage of it. I know that it does not matter if a freight train runs through the riding on the way to Vancouver at three o'clock in the morning, but it matters a great deal if passenger trains go through at such an ungodly hour.
We find another example on the very important run from Ottawa to Montreal. A few years ago it used to be a pleasure to take the train, have breakfast on the way, and get to the big city in time to do some business and take the train back- again in the evening. However, the railways decided that it was too much trouble serving mere passengers. They altered the schedules, took off the dining car and generally discouraged people from taking the train.
The government is spending tens of millions of dollars on an experiment to initiate the world's first downtown to downtown STOL airplane service between major cities. While this is certainly a step in the direction of providing adequate service between cities, it is still not a complete substitute for adequate rail passenger service between Canada's major cities and areas. In fact, Mr. Speaker, the government talks about using the new STOL service in order to prove that our aircraft industry can make a better
Transportation
STOL plane than anyone else, so that we can sell airplanes.
Just a couple of years ago we were involved in fierce debate over whether the two major rail systems in our country should be allowed to discontinue transcontinental passenger rail service. It was found then that the railways wanted to concentrate on freight service and gradually scale down passenger service to the point where people would just get tired of the whole mess and use the planes and buses. We just squeaked through that one and ended up with minimum transcontinental rail passenger service. But we in Parry Sound-Muskoka still do not have anywhere near the service we need and should have.
Everyone in this House knows that our highways are getting to the point where they are clogged with traffic almost around the clock. This means that people are burning gasoline at a greater rate than they should, and it means also that the incidence of highway deaths and injuries is rising yearly at an alarming rate. Automobile repairs and write-offs amount to hundreds of millions of dollars, and this is reflected in increased insurance premiums. I can speak with some authority on that as an insurance agent.
Adequate rail passenger service from cities like Toronto to outlying areas such as the Muskoka lakes vacationland would take hundreds and possibly thousands of automobiles off the roads, especially on weekends. I do not believe that anyone in his or her right mind would consider driving an automobile between these points unless it were absolutely necessary; therefore, proper train service would take much of the necessity out of this type of driving.
It is said trains run at a loss, but if there were a special rate for a vacationland train of this type it would pay its way, and would be filled to capacity.
Most of the stations in my area have been torn down, abandoned or replaced with a small leanto that could only be termed as a backhouse. There are no lights, and you have to stand out and try to flag down the passenger train as it goes through.
The railways are concentrating most of their efforts on providing freight service while scaling down passenger service, and even the freight and express service are not all that they should be. During the last strike, because there was no express train service the Grey Coach Lines started a parcel delivery service, and they are still in that in a big way. Buses going north are loaded because they are giving fast, guaranteed service.
Industries and businesses in small areas are not able to ship goods by rail because of the high cost of freight. As was mentioned earlier today in the House, short run freight rates are prohibitive. If something could be done to streamline freight rates I am sure it would be to the advantage of the railways. Of course they do not have too much competition. The two main companies own trucking services-in other words, you have to deal with the railway whether you ship by rail, car or tractor trailer transport.
The countries of western Europe have better railway service than we have in Canada even if they do not have the distances to contend with that we have in our country,

with its vast areas and distances between major cities. Yet the railway is still the best means of transport, or at least it would be if we could have adequate and dependable rail service.
We hear today that with the airlines also, freight service is increasing at a faster rate than passenger service, and most airlines are using combination passenger-freight aircraft. In fact even some of the jumbo jets, designed for passenger services, are being converted into freight carriers.
This morning's Globe and Mail featured a story on its front page telling of how passengers on Air Canada flights to Toronto were landed in Montreal and abandoned to their fates. They were not fed, nor were they given any assistance in getting to the destinations for which they had bought tickets. It seems that the Air Canada officials felt that, as long as they landed their passengers somewhere in Canada, then they should be satisfied.
This diversion was made necessary because the runways at Toronto International Airport were covered with snow, and the runway cleaners were on strike. A spokesman for Air Canada was reported as saying that Air Canada could not accept responsibility for passengers whose flights were interrupted for reasons beyond Air Canada's control. It was also reported that passengers bound for Toronto on CP Air were fed when they landed at Montreal, and were afterwards sent on to Toronto by bus.
The government-owned airline seems to have the same attitude toward people as the government-owned railway, and this can only be explained as a lack of government transportation policy. It could mean also that the government-owned airline is more interested today in hauling freight than in serving passengers. Whatever the reason, let me tell the House that if I ever buy a ticket on Air Canada for a certain destination and get dumped in some other place, then I shall be talking to the minister or to the Air Canada officials about it.
I do not know whether the Minister of Transport will even get the point of what this opposition day is all about, but I do know one thing; we in the opposition will not fail to let the minister and the government know, on a day-today basis, that the Canadian people are getting fed up with not having a national transportation policy. They are fed up with being treated worse than cattle and grain when they travel on our railways and airlines. People deserve better, and if the minister does not feel that he can create some order out of the confusion in his department, I suggest that he do the decent thing and resign.

Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure to join in this debate on the extremely important question of transportation, and particularly to follow immediately the observation of the hon. member opposite that "we are very concerned about the need in Canada for a transportation policy." Those words are very interesting. How often do members of the opposition use those words, and then immediately point to what they mean by them by indicating that there is a clear need for an additional airport runway in the village Podunk in

order to make Canada's transportation policy perfectly effective.
The members of the opposition express their interest in transportation matters by asking the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) about things such as that-an individual runway here, a particular subdivision there, and the line of a report some place else. I suppose this is a fairly classic opposition tactic, to attempt to make it seem that the minister should know about each of these small details, matters that in fact are only suitable for the order paper.
The fact of the matter is that such individual details cannot and should not be in the forefront of the mind of the Minister of Transport, who is attempting to formulate and develop an over-all policy for transportation in Canada within federal jurisdiction. The concern of the opposition about these petty and minor matters distracts from some other rather key issues.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) pointed out today what I think everyone should recognize, and that is that with our tremendous geographic problems, problems that make transportation an important, indeed essential element in this country, we have by and large been reasonably successful with our transportation system. Our criticisms of the system are really related to our desire for a better system, rather than contrasting how the job is done in other countries.
At the present time the opposition are concentrating on individual, minor issues. They are trying, as they have tried before, to make something strange out of the fact that because of my responsibility for grain and connection with the grains group, and because of my role in which I work closely with the Minister of Transport regarding the handling and transport of grain, both the Minister of Transport and I are interested in the same important subject matter.
I say it is an important subject matter; about one quarter of the ton miles of freight hauled in Canada is of grain. We have seen the railway perform this task extremely well during the past several years. While we have had labour troubles and have encountered other difficulties in trying to achieve internationally new and record goals, we have none the less achieved these goals.
I should remind hon. members that in the year 1972-73, notwithstanding significant closedowns because of labour and other problems, such as cold weather and difficulty getting through the Rockies, the railway system in this country moved over 800 million bushels of grain for export and in total close to one billion bushels of grain were transported, an amount never before achieved.
We have also made great improvements to the rail system in the matter of grain handling. Things like hopper cars, the block system and co-ordinators at terminals are all part of trying to make the system work more efficiently. Hon. members should be aware as well that one of the reasons transportation is such a massive responsibility, one that cannot be within the knowledge and purview of the Minister of Transport to the last detail, is that in this country we have developed a transportation system where we rely on the individual responsibility of the various parties to, and parts of, that system. It is not for the
March 10, 1975

Minister of Transport to endeavour to try to run the railways or to run Air Canada. It is not as though he should be involved in every one of the system's facets. The system must always run with reliance placed upon the responsibility of the various individuals throughout the system; and the role of the government, and therefore that of the minister, is one of over-all co-ordination and development of planning to see that all goes well.
Under the present Minister of Transport development of planning and policy has been moving forward like never before. Here, of course, is a major area where the opposition has an extremely legitimate and useful role to play, namely, in putting forward to the government major policy considerations. I think it has, too, the responsibility and opportunity to repeat to us time and time again the promises and pledges we have made regarding a major overhaul of the transportation system. It is therefore not surprising that the opposition wants at this point in time to show impatience at the kind of job being done.
The important thing to remember, Mr. Speaker, is that as those promises are carried out and as those pledges are implemented, our national policy will show its new form in terms of developing the kind of transportation system that we need. That is what the work of transportation is all about at the present time. It is a matter of major planning, of such issues as the control of rates in this country for freight, and of determining a new technique. We are not satisfied with the technique of the past.
Let me remind hon. members that no one in the House should treat this matter as though it were a simple and easy one. We cannot expect solutions to be found and implemented overnight.

I remind the House, and the Conservative member who says "huh," that during the term of office of several years of the Conservative government under the right hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker) the only step taken in terms of a transportation policy for Canada was the creation of a royal commission, which itself sat for six or seven years before reporting. Hon. members will also notice that that party does not propose specific solutions but only agrees that the problem has been fairly stated by the government and that, therefore, solutions have to be found.
It is important that we find an appropriate mechanism for controlling the level of freight rates and relating them in some way to reasonable total costs and not leaving the railways free, as they have been largely under the law up to this point, to be limited only by competition. Where there is competition, and by not very satisfactory rules where there is no competition, rules which do not always hold the charges anywhere near total cost. We are not happy with that. A solution to that is what we are seeking. However, we will not pretend that the solution is easy. I challenge hon. members opposite to find one and put it

forward if they in fact think it is so easy. It cannot be done.
These are important issues. And so is our pledge that there should be removal of inequities in freight rates, and we are going about this in the way the complex problem deserves.
If members opposite want to criticize, the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand) may be doing so much consultation with the provinces upon these issues that he is being that much more thorough in order to bring them along with the matters he is undertaking and studying. However, hon. members know full well if he were doing any less, that would be the front upon which the attack would be aimed. It is obvious he is doing exactly what he ought to in order to bring the provinces along to find solutions, in bringing about fair and equitable freight rates.
Members opposite talk in support of the principles of equity of freight rates. More specifically, I have heard them talk about the importance of and agreeing with the principle in our feed grains policy of producing equity in freight rates between meat and grain. They will say that, but not a word will they say about the manner in which they think it ought to be brought about, the issue that we obviously have to tackle in order to solve the problem.
The only solution of those who think they can do it safely politically is to suggest if there is a low cost freight rate on grain, then obviously a low rate on meat is desirable. However, this will involve further large payments from the treasury in order to support the rail costs that are involved over and above that low rate.

That is a serious proposition I put before hon. members, one we ought to be debating to try to determine the sort of program we should have in developing our transportation policy in this country. Those who want to agitate farmers about the Crowsnest rate should listen again to what I have said. No one is threatening the Crowsnest rate. Mr. Speaker, I am glad to participate in this debate, particularly since we witnessed this afternoon the performance of two lieutenants apparently sent to bail out the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marchand). I thought this was a transport debate. Apparently we are yet to hear from the Minister of Transport, who also spoke last Friday, but his arguments at that time certainly did not deal with transportation. They dealt with everything but the problem of transportation. That shows the attitude of this minister and why we are concerned about how that department is being administered. The minister is not running the department. That is our concern.
We heard a very good presentation by the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson). He brought the debate on track. He concerned himself with transport problems. Why could not the Minister of Transport have done the same-after all, he is supposed to have the authority? He is head of the department and answers for it.
From time to time members have risen to question the minister about specific items. There is no point in elaborating upon them all, but I remember being concerned some years ago about the fact that locomotives were not equipped with flashers. I was told that a study was being conducted, but that is as far as I got. I was told that the cost of equipping locomotives with flashers was prohibitive-that it would amount to something like $700 per locomotive. I imagine it would be more like $2,000 today. Anyway, the minister said that studies were being conducted, and that is as far as the matter went. What was the result of those studies? What was the point in conducting them?
The transportation problem we face in Western Canada has already been well documented. Member after member has given an account of what has happened to shipments of cattle from western to eastern Canada in contrast to shipments of meat. As everyone knows, a conference was held in Calgary. It was supposed to seek solutions to the problems which have so long been irking the people of western Canada. The minister was told the nature of these grievances, as if he needed to be told; every year for the last 20 years successive Liberal governments have been told that the basic complaint is the existence of grave inequities in the freight rate structure.
To dramatize his concern the minister called a western conference, in the course of which all these difficulties were once again outlined. At the end of the conference, a communique was issued and the western spokesmen sat back and waited for further developments. The premiers who took part in this conference expected a lot from the minister. They said a break-through might finally have been achieved. From all indications, it should have been. But a minister must do something when an opportunity is presented to him. He cannot just sit on his hands.
I once had a teacher who told us in class, "If you cannot solve a problem, forget it. Otherwise you are like a hen sitting on a rotten egg. You will never hatch a chick out of
March 10, 1975

it." The Minister of Transport just shrugs his shoulders while another minister bails him out. Then the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) has to get involved because he is an authority on justice, an authority on the Wheat Board, and the be all and end all as far as transport is concerned.
One dictator in the cabinet is enough. I do not think we need another. The Minister of Justice has enough problems in his own department. He should leave transportation to the Minister of Transport. Why does he come out with transport proposals affecting Western Canada? We deal in more than agricultural products. There is sulphur, there is potash, there are minerals, all kinds of things. The Minister of Justice takes it upon himself to be the western spokesman. What a mess he is making of it. He himself started the debate on the Crowsnest pass agreement. No one else thought of tampering with it. The man who is supposed to be the western representative in the cabinet proposed doing away with the Crowsnest agreement because of the fact that cattlemen in Western Canada find themselves in a difficult position.
The government says, "Let us take this concession away from the grain farmers and give it to the cattlemen, because the cattlemen passed a resolution at their conference asking for extra consideration on the grounds that if there is a special rate for grain they should get a lower rate, too." Granted the cattlemen have reason to complain, but why take anything away from the grain farmers? For once they are getting an improved standard of living, and now the minister wants to take it away. And there is every indication that he will succeed.
Let us go back into history. There was a commission set up to inquire into transportation, and this commission came up with certain recommendations. That was some time ago. The minister talks about seven years. It is almost seven years now since the freeze was imposed. The freeze was put on in 1970 and it is coming to an end in 1975 by which time, maybe, that study should have been completed. The commission had one specific problem to deal with, and it has taken five years already. Another year is coming up rapidly, yet the minister has told us that a seven year period was too long for a transport study under a Conservative government. Why should we need that extra year? The government should have had a policy ready.
The reason I am taking part in this debate is that we have a block system and the minister has some responsibility for seeing that grain is moved. He says everything is rosy, but the facts are otherwise. Why is not greater use being made of the facilities at the Port of Churchill? Let me give an illustration of what I have in mind. The town of Norquay is closer to Churchill than are many communities in Assiniboia. Nevertheless the railways will not ship grain from Norquay though they are willing to do so from Assiniboia, perhaps as a reward for its electing a Liberal member. There is a shortage of boxcars. Everybody realizes we can transport grain from a large number of communities in Western Canada to Churchill and have the cars back within a couple of days. But they prefer to take the grain from distant communities; the cars take a week to go to Churchill and a week to come back. That is the way the system is being managed.
Transportation
A few weeks ago I asked what was happening about freight rates. In the communities near Hudson Bay freight rates have shot up by 500 per cent, reaching an unrealistic level as far as many Canadians are concerned. We complain about 25 per cent. The government intervened and reduced the increase to 12 Vfc per cent. This time the minister says he does not have the power to intervene. Yet when the increase of 25 per cent was in effect the minister did reduce it. So, what is he talking about when he says he does not have power under the existing act? I suggest the power is there, but there is no drive or willingness on the part of the government to act on these problems.
Let me illustrate what has happened in those small communities. They were getting their wholesale commodities in from Prince Albert. Before the increase went into effect on February 24, I believe it was, fresh meat came in at $1.89 per cwt. Smoked meat and bacon came in at $1.33 per cwt. and groceries came in under third class at $1.05. Then the railways came in with the new regulations. First of all they locked the rates altogether in one class, and then proceeded to impose the new rates. The new rate this time in respect of groceries jumped from $1.05 to $4.97. What kind of a percentage increase is that? This is much, much more than a 25 per cent increase, and no one needs a calculator to figure that one out.
The minister asks what our problem is and why the west is complaining. He says the government is doing everything it can within its power. I would ask the minister if the government is really doing everything in its power? If the government is concerned about western economic opportunities, and development in that part of the country, perhaps it should establish a branch within the Department of Transport which could work very closely with the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion.
There are possibilities for development in this country, particularly in the west, but we need some co-ordination, and we must have some willingness on the part of the government to tackle these problems. In all the years I have been in this House I have never heard anyone complain when preferential freight rates have been adopted for the Atlantic region. We all know this is an area which requires special attention, and we are willing to give people there that assistance. I think the same thing is true of western Canada.
I suggest that what we are concerned about is when the government gives this type of assistance to that small circle in central Canada, which has a natural geographic preference in any event. The government does everything it can, from every angle, to improve the lot of those people in that small area. The government always looks after them, and I find that this has been true over the years. However, when it comes to improving the situation in western Canada or in the Atlantic area, the government is not quite so willing to act, and I think there is general agreement in that regard among hon. members in this House, no matter which province they represent.
The situation which exists in respect of it being cheaper to ship from central Canada to Vancouver than it is to Regina has been pointed out on many occasions. The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion has asked what
3960

March 10, 1975
Transportation
the members and the people from British Columbia will say to preferential rates for the prairies. I suggest this does not have to be the federal policy. It would be all right for provincial governments to take this stand in order to improve the economic environment of individual provinces, but I do not think it should be federal government policy to discriminate deliberately against any region. Even if the government moves only one-half a step at a time toward resolving these discriminatory rates, that will be a move in the right direction.
The cost of shipping freight from central Canada to Regina should at no time be higher than the rate to Vancouver, but that is the situation that exists today. Even if the cost were the same it would not be fair, but at least then we would be removing half the discrimination, and instead of having a half a dozen burrs we would have only three.
I could go on to describe what is happening in general transportation policy so far as Churchill is concerned. Several years ago there was an item in the Blue Book in respect of development at Churchill. Everybody got excited because certain funds were allocated for this purpose. Because of a squabble that began between the officials of the department and some members of the Hudson Bay Route Association, that development never proceeded.
We now may well have a similar situation in disguise, but unless the government intends to proceed with its announced intention there is no point in fooling the people. A tremendous savings could be effected through the use of Churchill as an export port. There is a railway in existence at the moment that could be utilized. The CPR should certainly be allowed running rights by the CNR, and the CNR should be forced to make use of this line. We should always follow the shortest route to the port requiring the shortest period of travel time. I suggest there is no need for a duplication of services or the abandonment of many of these particular rail lines.
After five years of study what did this government come up with? It has put a freeze until the year 2,000 on abandonment in relation to some 13,000 miles of rail line. There is still some 6,000 miles of rail lines in question. We are not concerned about the 500 odd miles on which there is agreement for abandonment. Those are not the lines that one should be concerned about at this time. Nor should we be concerned now about the 13,000 miles that will be frozen, but it should be of immediate concern to hon. members that 6,000 miles are still in question.
What should be our immediate priorities in respect to this proposed rail line abandonment? I suggest the government must indicate to the communities concerned what is planned. There certainly must be co-operation between the federal government, the provincial governments and the local communities. The government must make known its intention in respect of upgrading these lines.
This involves another matter. No one has ever proven to me, or to many of the people involved, that there was ever anything wrong with the roadbeds in question. I suggest that the railways over a period of time have allowed those roadbeds to deteriorate, always keeping in the back of their minds the desire to abandon certain lines. Do hon. members know what transpired during the last five-year freeze on rail line abandonments? I suggest all this did

was give the railways time to allow a few more lines to deteriorate to the point that they should be abandoned. That is all that came out of the last freeze.
A study in respect of all these problems should have been carried out and completed by now. All these communities should have been asked to state their problems and how they think they should be resolved. They should have been asked how they think the railways could meet the proposed highway programs which will have to be met if the railways are to discontinue this service. These people should know what facilities will be available for servicing their communities, but nothing like that has ever been indicated.
The railways have held general meetings at certain central points, at which a fast talking public relations man has attempted to illustrate to the few people who were able to attend, perhaps 100 miles from the community affected, that everything is going to be all right, just give the railways the opportunity and they will prove it. It has never been proven that the service has been improved as a result of the abandonment of any rail line. That has never been proven to the satisfaction of the people involved; those people have had to live with the situation.
We are talking about 6,000 miles of proposed rail line abandonment. That is a lot of line, and a lot of people are affected. This is the type of irritation that must be corrected. Transportation has been a very important factor in the development of the west. Transportation can be made to work for the west and for all of Canada, but we need a minister and a government that are willing to come up with solutions to the problems and act on them.
