speechtext:
Since I came to this House I have always wondered why British Columbia was prosperous. I agonized about this until this afternoon when the hon. member for Stormont-Dundas (Mr. Lumley) told me why.
March 10,1975

It is not difficult; it is because of the policies of the Minister of Transport when he was Minister of Regional Economic Expansion. That is what happened.
It was because of all that wonderful industrial development which came about. I should like to tell the hon. member for Stormont-Dundas that the province of British Columbia in 1973 received one per cent of the amount of DREE money that went out from Ottawa. Out of an amount of $450 million we received $4 million. Between 1969 and 1973 the total amount received by British Columbia in DREE grants was $16 million while the federal government was spending $500 million a year. Many people talk about separatism in this country. I agree that there is a lack of understanding between one part of the country and the other, but it is a two-way street. When I hear a member from Ontario talk about that it seems to me that he has less understanding of my province than I have of his.
I also listened with great interest to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lang) most energetically and eloquently defend the Minister of Transport tonight. In fact he was so eloquent and energetic that I suspect he is preaching for a call over there. I want to tell you, Mr. Speaker, that I would not be unhappy with that switch. Today the hon. member for York East (Mr. Collenette) suggested that we need time in which to develop these policies. He said we require time in which to look at it and to do something about it.
I wish to give this House a brief history. There was something called the Darling report, which is a pretty significant part of the minister's responsibility. This report came out in 1970. Back on May 26, 1971, in this House the then hon. member for Saint John-Lancaster asked the Minister of Transport of that date, the present Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson), a question on this matter, to which the minister replied:
I agree that it is a 'Darling' report. We will do our very best to implement as quickly as possible those parts of it which seem to have public favour.
Then again in respect of the same report on June 8, 1971, the minister gave this reply to a question:
Just as soon as we have these views, government policy will be formulated along these lines. X would hesitate to give a time frame, but perhaps by the autumn of this year might be a reasonable expectation.
Those were the answers by the minister in respect of the Darling report at that time. That is the kind of action we received from the previous minister. I can understand his defending this Minister of Transport so vigorously because his record is not much to write home about. As we move through this time frame we come to the present minister.
In respect of the Darling report, in 1973 the present minister had some comment to make. I cannot find his comments in my papers but I know he said something in 1973 about bringing down government policy very shortly. The reason many of us are concerned about the Darling report and its implementation-and the minister has indicated his interest in seeing it implemented-is that we have lost control of our shipping for a very long time.
If that report were implemented 40,000 jobs would be created in this country, at a time of rising unemployment. There is no doubt this is one of the specific things that
Transportation
need not wait for an over-all study and could be undertaken quickly, but this has not been done. That is one of the criticisms by the opposition. It not only would create 40,000 jobs but would give some impact to the Law of the Sea Conference. We are now going into this conference and there is a fairly good chance that we will have a 200-mile limit. What will Canada do in terms of coastal shipping? We will still have foreign navigation bottoms off our coast carrying Canadian goods. The implementation of the recommendations contained in this report is long overdue. We now have a second Darling report in respect of deep sea shipping. Will it take as long a period to consider this report before we will have a Canadian merchant marine? I expect this will take even longer.
Another aspect of the minister's policy is that it is easier to buy a ship in this country if you do not buy it for Canadian purposes than it is if you are a Canadian user of that vessel, because under the Export Development Corporation the terms for the borrowing of money are much more advantageous. The Darling report pointed out that this is a major failure in terms of our policy.
I wish to refer briefly to another phase of transportation. I refer to the ferry system in this country. Under the present ferry system most of the ferries are subsidized in one way or another by the federal government. The Trans-Canada Highway begins where I come from, on the coast of British Columbia. The only gap is across the Straits of Georgia. Not a dime has been received from the federal government in the form of a subsidy in respect of that ferry system. There are construction subsidies but there is nothing in terms of a subsidy for operation or for the building of terminal facilities. I know the answer of the minister is that because it is not an interprovincial ferry it does not come under federal jurisdiction.

One of the reasons we did not do very well was the kind of promises that were made to the Canadian people by my friends in the government. They promised a policy, they promised some action and some leadership. In the speech from the throne in the twenty-ninth parliament they went so far as to promise an improvement in the total transportation system so basic to overcoming the problems of distance. In the twenty-ninth parliament, on February 27, the minister promised that steps would be taken to end discrimination in freight rates.
Then, on March 7, the minister said in the House that transportation is a problem so important to the future of the country that we should at least look into each others eyes and say what we really think about this matter. Finally the minister told us that he really thought on January 22, 1975, when he said that we have no over-all policy, that it is still in a mess and more a mess than we think.
What kind of a reaction can members of the opposition have to such a statement in the House? I appreciate the minister's frankness, but where is the leadership? That is what we are looking for, Mr. Speaker. It is all right to say that things are in a mess, but you must try to do something about that. That is what we are going to get in the next election, another promise.

Mr. Speaker, to be fair I must say that I am not referring to my hon. colleague-

speechtext:
I think that the hon. Leader of the Opposition is an honourable man. He will take my word that I never referred to the House. On the contrary, the only place where it is clear is here, and it is in Hansard. When I was talking outside the House-and some day I will say it openly-I excluded the House and I excluded the whole opposition, and I say that the debate did not take place on racism. I regret, but I do not think hon. members have the right to make an accusation of that kind. I do not believe that the hon. member is a racist.
I wish to talk about transportation, and I do not feel that I was dealt with justly on this matter. I wanted the situation to be clear, and I tried to clarify it.
I have been accused of having recourse to my friend the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson), the former minister of transport, to help me out this afternoon. I did it first because he is intelligent. He knows
Transportation
something about transport, and as I had already spoken on Friday, I thought perhaps there would be a better balance this way. I know that I have shortcomings, but I do not think that fear is one of them.
I do not think it will be a big problem for me to talk for another ten minutes. I can do this if you want to sit and listen. This is not the problem. The problem is a problem of transportation. We promised during the election that we would transform the system; we were not satisfied with the system, we are not yet satisfied with the system. But the main opposition complaint-and during the debate I understood that I should have been more careful about this-is that I have not kept the House sufficiently well informed about the kind of work that is being done in my ministry. This is something that the opposition could not have found out by themselves without being told. I will think about that to see to what extent it is feasible to remedy this.
I think it would be interesting for hon. members to know of all those who are at work right now on very specific problems, trying to find solutions so that we can have a national transportation policy. Let us call it transportation policies for Canada because there is no doubt that the policy for the Maritimes is not the policy for the Arctic, it is not the policy for Quebec, it is not the policy for Ontario nor for the west, and it is not the policy for British Columbia. This means that we have to find solutions to each of those problems, and I am working on them.
Hon. members say that it takes a long time, and they are right, but just look at the history of this department-not only this department, but almost everything we have ever done here in the House. Just think how long it took-and I remember my hon. friend from St. John's East (Mr. McGrath) asking when we would produce the act-to create the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. I think that is the role of the opposition and I do not complain, but the MacPherson report took seven years before being tabled in the House, and we waited about ten years, or not far from ten years for Mr. Justice Bernier in Quebec to complete a report on pilotage.
If there has been a mistake I think this is where it is; perhaps I could have kept the House better informed, not of results but of what we have been doing. When it is said that nothing has been done, I do not believe it, and the opposition does not believe it. That is probably the right way to attack the government, and I would probably do the same thing.
We have done a lot of things in the field of transport in British Columbia. My hon. friend opposite suggested that we look at regional development because he considered that too much was being given to eastern Canada and not enough to the west. Do not forget that British Columbia has had things the maritimes did not get. Just remember Roberts Bank; just remember the money we spent on the harbour in Vancouver, and the development of the harbour in the north, Prince Rupert, the opening of roads, and so forth. If we are going to have a balance sheet in this country in order to know which section of this country is getting most from the federal government, if we are going to try to do that we will kill this country because everyone profits in this country, but not all in the same way.

March 10, 1975

subsubtopic: ALLOTTED DAY S.O. 58-ALLEGED GOVERNMENT FAILURE TO PRESENT CO-ORDINATED TRANSPORTATION POLICY
speechtext:
Not all, excuse me, but on a large number of goods, by truck or by train. We still have the intra-subsidy, which of course is being phased out. The Port of Halifax is being developed faster than ever before. The average income in Halifax is now higher than in Montreal, and that is true also of Saint John, New Brunswick.
Certain things have changed, but I do not claim that we have changed everything. We have the problem of the ferries in the maritimes. We have been working with the government of Newfoundland and we are going to have two new ships, and a new ship for Wood Island and Prince Edward Island. We have brought back the boat that goes between Digby and Saint John because the CP refused to operate it effectively. We are solving the problem of the ferry between Yarmouth and Bar Harbor in the United States. We have done a lot of things for that region, Mr. Speaker.
We have worked with provincial ministers and officials and have accomplished a great deal. We are working on highways, amongst other things. In Quebec the Mirabelle airport will be open in a few months time. Of course some people do not like airports, but there is nothing I can do about that.
I was listening to the speech of the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) and I should like to tell him that one month from now Air Canada, at the request of the government of Saskatchewan, is going to produce a plan for a regional air carrier. He did not know that, but I know it.

In my own office we are working hard on this policy. There is a special core group studying all the problems of transportation. The deputy minister has an advisory committee, there is a task force, an interdepartmental participation committee, federal-provincial consultations and consultations with industry,

trucking, railways and airlines. We are trying to put all that together to formulate a policy in order to serve Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, a general statement is made that nothing is done in the area of transportation. When I said transportation was a mess I meant thait coordination was not there. It is still not there for that matter, and that was the work I had to continue when Mr. Jamieson was Minister of Transport.
The CTC is a kind of Crown corporation with enormous independence. The St. Lawrence Seaway Authority is a corporation almost equally independent. Air Canada has even the authority to buy houses in Barbados from what I can see, and without my authorization. The CNR is an extremely independent company, and the same goes for the Northern Transportation Corporation. Then you have three great authorities within the department-for air, for land and for sea. I heard a Progressive Conservative member say this afternoon that all that is very funny but I know there are people who put their hearts and souls into trying to find the best system possible for Canada, the one which will make this country even more prosperous. For example, we have the whole far north to develop, we are making plans to build a cargo that will also be an icebreaker and will be able to help develop the whole far north of Canada.

Mr. Speaker, in the brief time I have I should like to devote my remarks to Air Canada operations, but first I should like to correct some comments made by the hon. member for St. Boniface (Mr. Guay) on Friday, March 7. At page 3906 of Hansard, he said:
The safety record of Air Canada is similar to the safety record of the CNR,... members of the Conservative Party ...
He was referring to me.
seem to get some kind of sadistic satisfaction from continually accusing the airline in respect of its safety performance.
The hon. member for St. Boniface seems to be mixed up. Last February during an adjournment debate he remarked that I was to be lauded for my concern about passenger safety. He changed his mind over that, fast. Then he went on to say that he was amazed at people like me continuing to paint the worst possible picture of our country's flag carrier. He said I had never taken the trouble to accept an invitation to inspect Air Canada's servicing facilities. We have been over all this before, Mr. Speaker, even on April 23, 1974. I have spoken numerous times in the House on the subject and I have travelled to Dorval and reviewed the situation of employees there, many of whom I am in constant touch with, and I do not know why we are bringing this up again, Mr. Speaker.
March 10, 1975

These remarks in regard to safety are not mine; they come from unions, from employees, from newspaper articles. When I spoke in the adjournment debate last week I referred to articles like the one in the Montreal Gazette, a headline story on air safety. These articles do not refer only to Air Canada but to all regional airlines. This is the type of document the hon. member and the hon. minister should be reading.
I have here a document sent to the director of maintenance quality signed by eight shop inspectors at Dorval. They state:
Attached to this letter, please find a submission related to the unit and Support Shops Inspections Functions. It is a critical report presented in the interest of achieving a more effective inspection program and hopefully to create an awareness of an existing low morale condition.
There follow four pages of a condemning attack on Air Canada dealing with all kinds of problems with audits, manuals and what-have-you.
I also have a union document which states that the supervisor's only concern is in trying to run a scheduled operation at all costs. The results of this attitude causes one of their larger problems and one of the most frequent violations of the collective agreement, namely, safety. The collective agreement is quite clear in that management is specifically charged with the duty of initiating and monitoring all practices necessary to ensure the safety and health of employees, as well as ensuring the safety of all equipment. They go to say that because of the attitude of first level supervision and refusal to initiate safety the shop committee is handling the problem.
These are not my comments, Mr. Speaker. These are the comments in a union publication put out at Dorval Airport. This is why we are calling for a full scale investigation into Air Canada. Instead of giving us a series of alibis and excuses as to why the government should not do anything, the minister should go to Dorval and speak to these people.
Let me give another example. Members of parliament are continually receiving telegrams about the air finance branch in Winnipeg.
